Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In the four years between 1976 and 1980, 1,810 Indian women lost their Indian status under Section 12(l)(b) of the Indian Act, which clause has been declared discriminatory by the United Nations Human Rights Commission.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Were that family living in the United States its cost of living increase would be $50 per month less than it is in Canada. The Secretary of State indicated that the problems facing Canadians are wholly due to international situations. If this is so, how does the minister explain to a family such as I have mentioned why they are $50 per month worse off in Canada because of inflation than their counterparts in the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

Madam Speaker, knowing the Secretary of State as well as I do, and knowing his deep understanding of the economy, I do not believe he would say that our problems were solely due to international events.
Obviously, what is happening in our traditional markets and what is happening to American interest rates are all factors which affect Canadians very adversely. That is a fact of life. But it is true that the performance of the American economy on the inflation front is better than Canada's. Not only is the cost of living index in the United States much lower than ours, the average wage settlement at the present time is from 4 percentage points to 7 percentage points lower in the United States than in Canada. That is why, if we are to remain competitive and create more jobs in Canada, as is our principle objective, we must do everything possible to reduce our inflation rate even further.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. The minister will know that he initiated the uranium cartel prosecution based upon the results of the Bertrand report and upon the sworn affidavit of Mr. Orest R. Samitz, a combines investigation officer who believed that there was a conspiracy to fix the prices of uranium. On Friday afternoon last the Supreme Court of Ontario decided that Crown corporations were immune from prosecution. The shocking implication of this is that the courts of this country do not have jurisdiction over potential illegalities or criminal offences of Crown corporations. Since there is no accountability by the criminal courts of this country with respect to Crown corporations, will the minister make the Bertrand report public? Also, will he release us from the gag rule which has been an impediment to free speech since 1976?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: URANIUM PRICE FIXING TRIAL-POSITION OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this morning we decided to appeal the decision of the Supreme Court of Ontario, and the case is now before a higher court. As for the Bertrand report, there were, of course, two things we could do: either take legal action, which we have done, or refer the report, as was done in the case of the oil companies, to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. In this case, which concerns the uranium question, we decided to bring the matter directly before the courts, where it is now. After the decision by the Supreme Court of Ontario on Friday, counsel for the Canadian government decided to appeal.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in this particular prosecution the conduct of the Minister of Justice has been absolutely disgraceful.
Oh, oh!
It has been absolutely disgraceful.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Like Jack Austin?

Where is the fairness in having private corporations prosecuted in circumstances where public corporations, Crown corporations, are immune from prosecution? Secondly, prior to the prosecution being initiated, was the minister not aware that Crown corporations could not be prosecuted because they were immune, and is that why he did not charge the officers of the company?
April 26, 1982

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have answered this question several times before. At the Department of Justice, on the advice of counsel who had served as such on the Bertrand Commission, we decided to take both the private sector and public sector people to court. That is what we have done. A decision was handed down by the Ontario Supreme Court Friday, and, Madam Speaker, I cannot change the laws of this country. The case is before the Ontario Court of Appeal, and we have followed the procedure prescribed by the laws of Canada. When we receive a report from the Director of Investigation and Research, either we take legal action or we refer the case to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. We have taken one of these options. The court has handed down a decision, and we are appealing that decision because, at the time, we decided that legal action had to be taken against both private and public sector companies. Energy Administration Act
constituency of Leeds-Grenville and, if so, what would be the merit in transferring authority to the Department of Employment and Immigration at the port of Lansdowne outside the area of Leeds-Grenville to the port of Kingston?
2.	Was it customary for immigration at Lansdowne, the Ontario Provincial Police at Gananoque and Brockville and the RCMP at Brockville to maintain close liaison with the immigration centre located at Prescott in the constituency of Leeds-Grenville and, if so, what advantage could there be in placing immigration at Lansdowne, under the authority of the port of Kingston, outside the constituency of Leeds-Grenville, which has never been involved with Lansdowne?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
1. Persons arrested for immigration infractions are arrested by immigration officers; RCMP and the OPP may subsequently lay charges if a violation of the Criminal Code is involved.
2.	There was and is no specific close liaison between the immigration personnel at Lansdowne with that of immigration at Prescott other than that normally experienced between all immigration points of service. Naturally, it is customary for all immigration points of service to maintain a good liaison with all enforcement agencies within their area of operation. There are several advantages in placing Lansdowne under the authority of the port of Kingston. Staff from Lansdowne will be immediately available for secondment to the Kingston inland centre during low traffic periods, affording better utilization of human resources at minimal costs and, thus, providing developmental exposure to border staff at a more complex inland office. The Ontario Provincial Police at Gananoque and Brockville and RCMP Brockville do maintain a liaison with Lansdowne. However, in most cases the OPP and RCMP contact Ottawa District office of CEIC to seek guidance on immigration cases.
3.	Such a move would neither involve delays in processing normal cases nor additional costs.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act

Madam Speaker, when I called it four o'clock on Friday I was in the course of trying to determine the factor for converting barrels into cubic metres or vice versa. As I recall, I was being assisted by a member other than the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), but I see that she is credited on page 16578 of Hansard with having provided the conversion factor. Be that as it may, I think it is worth while knowing what that factor is.
Can I ask for order, Mr. Speaker, please? There is more than one conversation going on at that end of the Elouse and I find it a little disconcerting.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I appreciate the hon. member's point. Perhaps, since he has brought his difficulty to the attention of the Elouse, he can now have the attention he wishes.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do believe the curtains were put there for a purpose. However, I will endeavour to override with my strident tones the conversations taking place.
I was about to say I thought it fortunate that I am covered by parliamentary immunity when 1 started talking about barrels and cubic metres and so on, because the notion of converting from one to the other is a dangerous operation these days. I learned, for example, that a carpet merchant on the west coast who displayed carpets at so much per square metre, but also had the temerity to advertise them simultaneously at so much per square foot or square yard, is now appearing before a judge because he has broken the law. So it is fortunate that we in this House are covered by parliamentary immunity and can still seek the conversion factor where necessary between barrels and cubic metres.
1 find it very helpful, when looking at a bill as complex as this one, to go through it extremely carefully and break it up into its various parts to determine just exactly what the thrust of the bill is. This bill now before us is in effect a copy, with certain important downward changes in tax limits, of the first 40 pages of the bill which caused the bells to ring, Bill C-94, with the exception of page 32 which has already appeared in Bill C-105. That is the iniquitous proposal which would authorize the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to spawn as many Crown corporations as he and his officials see fit, independent of Parliament. Even the annex in Bill C-103 has been transcribed faithfully-in cubic metres, mark you-from the earlier bill. The main intent of this bill is described in the explanatory notes. The purpose of this bill is, we read:
-to impose a charge on the export of crude oil and certain petroleum products, to provide compensation for certain petroleum costs and to regulate the price of Canadian crude oil and natural gas in interprovincial and export trade.
There are two purposes of this bill, one, to raise funds and the other, to regulate. Prior to having the bells to ring, we sought in our discussions, to have Bill C-94 broken down into
uniprinciple bills. Yet here we have one with two principles, to raise funds and to regulate.
One of the purposes of this bill is to raise funds, and as a result it deserves to be dealt with in a manner quite different from a regulatory bill. Because this bill has two principles, to raise funds and to regulate, I find it rather intolerable. In fact, it is an affront to Parliament to have these two particular principles in the same bill. At least though we were able to have the matter split from Bill C-94. Which in itself was an even more monstrous piece of legislation.
There are several kinds of taxes to be raised. I would like to deal with them separately if I can, not only to get them clear in my own mind, but also to keep them clear in the minds of all other Canadians who will have to pay some of those taxes.
First, the explanatory notes state that there is to be an oil export tax. That tax has been in effect for almost 18 months, in fact, since the October, 1980 budget. Its collection at current levels is in the first place to be retroactively legitimized and legalized. That is one of the first things Bill C-103 will do. It will legalize taxes now in place which have been in place since October, 1980. This export tax is, of course, levied at the international border. It forces the price of Canadian oil on the foreign market to higher and higher levels. Legally this oil export charge could be assessed at $8 a barrel but at the present time it is being levied at the rate of $25 per barrel. This is the first legalization procedure through which Bill C-103 takes us. It will legalize the current surcharge up to $25 a barrel. The limit that is placed on this particular levy in the bill, the limit to which the minister can go, will be $55 a barrel with increases at the discretion of the governor in council. I leave you, Mr. Speaker, to inquire how long our offshore markets will last if we double the current export tax level from $25 a barrel to $55 a barrel.
The other comment I have on this oil export charge is that nowhere does the bill specifically require the government to set up a fund into which the tax proceeds are to be fed; nor is there any clear statement as to "the certain petroleum costs" that are to be compensated from it. I find it rather odd for the bill to say that it is in order to compensate for certain petroleum costs and then not specify what those costs may be.
I still hear conversations going on in loud voices and in a very rude manner from the other side of the House.
Oh, oh!
On past experience, funds collected by this government, which has so many rude members who talk loudly in this House while others are trying to have themselves heard-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. May I draw to the attention of the hon. member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) wishes to address him and he would like his attention. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich.
April 26, 1982

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. On past experience, funds collected through taxes for certain purposes have all too often been funnelled off into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, there to be used for general purposes. We shall have to do everything possible in the consideration of this bill in committee to ensure that the oil export tax- sometimes, Mr. Speaker, I do wonder about the courtesy extended the members in this House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The Chair has no choice at this point. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has three times brought to the attention of the House and the Chair that he is unable to direct his remarks to the House because of the noise factor. I have to agree with the hon. member. If hon. members in the area where I am pointing feel it is necessary to carry on conversations, I would request them either to lower their voices or to solve the problem in some fashion in which the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich can be heard. He has brought the matter to the attention of the Chair three times.
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that. I suppose it is because of the conformation of the House in that particular corner which causes these echoes to occur here.
Oh, oh!

I do hope they will heed your admonition, Mr. Speaker.
My comment about the various sections of the bill causes me at this stage to leap over one of the tax levies in the bill. I will return to it in due course because it is a highly specialized one and it applies to a particular class of user. But the more important one and the next one I wish to examine is called the petroleum compensation charge. It may be that a number of those listening-and I hope some people are listening-are wondering why I am going over this matter by laying out a series of charges this bill will bring into being. But I want to make it clear that in the end the Canadian consumer, whether he drives a car or heats his house, is the one who will be paying these various charges. 1 am therefore breaking the bill down in this way to demonstrate that.
This petroleum compensation charge is levied at the processing level but it eventually works its way through the system. Owners of cars eventually pay for it whenever gas is pumped into their cars or oil is put into their furnaces. Canadians in the end pay this tax. The proceeds are intended to bridge the gap between domestic oil and offshore oil.
We may ask ourselves in 1982, since we have been talking about energy for as long as I can remember in this House and seeking self-sufficiency for just as long, why we are importing offshore oil? I have wondered about this for a long time. Here we see one of the major accomplishments of the bell-ringing operation early last month. Bill C-94, about which we were protesting so dramatically, set the charges for this petroleum compensation level at a maximum of $125 per cubic metre. Bill C-103 drops that limit to $75 per cubic metre. In other words, the bells rang and the government listened. It was a good thing that the government dropped the $125 charge contained in Bill C-94 to the $75 one in Bill C-103. Again I
Energy Administration Act
revert to more meaningful terms when I say from $20 per barrel to $12 per barrel. I guess it was worth keeping the bells ringing after all.
My second comment on this tax and its purpose is to draw the attention of the House to the fact that today we are needlessly importing 300,000 barrels of oil per day while cheaper domestic oil is locked into the ground. I do not know what madman devised the tax to pay for the importation of something which could be produced at home more cheaply. I just do not understand that type of reasoning. I would not be surprised if some Liberal members on the other side examined the bill and had difficulty understanding it. I suspect they have not examined it.
I do not think any apology is required for repeating something that was said by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) when he spoke to the bill last Wednesday. As reported at page 16480 of Hansard, he indicated that the misguided practice of importing and locking in 300,000 barrels of oil in Canada is costing Canadians $20 million per day. I questioned him at lunchtime as to whether he was sure about the figure. It is an outrageous figure, it comes to $7 billion per year which is being collected, from Canadians who are listening as well as those who are not listening, in order to pay for oil which we already have. Of course, we have to pay in United States funds, which puts a great strain on our exchange rate and the rate of inflation. I wonder whether Canadians have thought about its particular impact on the Canadian rate of exchange. A drain of that sort in United States funds, which have to be bought at 18, 19 or 20 per cent, is certainly considerable.
Why are we spending $20 million per day to import a product which we can produce in Canada and which will create jobs in Canada, rather than creating them in Venezuela, Saudi Arabia and Mexico? In any event, jobs are not being created in Canada, either in the east or in the west. Hon. members opposite still do not understand the idea that to choke and throttle the west is to choke and throttle the east, because the pipes and trucks are manufactured here. For one job lost in the west, two jobs are lost in the east. I see my hon. friend opposite giggling and waving; he just happens to fall in between.
Another tax to which I would like to refer is a specialized one. It is called the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. It is a long title which is supposed to be self-explanatory, but it is not quite. It appeared in the previous bill in this form, but as it contained certain peculiarities in its presentation, I decided to leave my consideration of it to this point. As its title almost suggests, this charge is to be levied on marine vehicles and aircraft fuelling in Canada but consuming their fuel on offshore routes. The bill provides only an upper limit of levy but gives no hint what the levy will be as of tomorrow or what the levy is today, for that matter. I suspect it is being

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
levied today. All of this is to be decided, as in some of the other instances, by the governor in council with the advice of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
The ceiling is set at $350 per cubic metre or $55 per barrel. Here again Parliament is being asked to turn over to two ministers of the government the power to set the levels of taxes. I think that principle is wrong. If the government wants to phase it in, it should be phased in in statute law as it indicated in other portions of the bill it is doing on the retroactive aspects of it. But I think the future aspects of it should be phased in by statute as well, and not left to the ministers or to the government to decide. Of course, these provisions like the others are retroactive. The levy has been collected since the budget of November 1980. Currently they run at $78 for marine diesel on the east coast and, peculiarly, at $47 for the same fuel on the west coast. There is no explanation here or anywhere which I have been able to discover as to why there is a differential in the charges for marine fuel on the east coast and on the west coast, with a high preference on the west coast for marine fuel being consumed in an offshore voyage. This is one matter which ought to be clarified by the minister in committee.
The charges for aircraft fuel and whether they vary across the country, I have been unable to discover. 1 hope there is ample opportunity in committee to inquire more closely into these matters.
There is one aspect of the bill which 1 think deserves some comment at this particular stage. 1 am wondering whether the definition of "offshore" on page 9 of Bill C-103, which is relevant to this particular levy, has been inserted in order to stake a claim for offshore jurisdiction. Clause 13(2) on page 9 reads in part as follows:
-"offshore area" means Sable Island or any area of land not within a province that belongs to Her Majesty in right of Canada or in respect of which Her Majesty in right of Canada has the right to dispose of or exploit the natural resources and that is situated in those submarine areas adjacent to the coast of Canada and extending throughout the natural prolongation of the land territory of Canada to the outer edge of the continental margin or to a distance of 200 nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea of Canada is measured, whichever is greater;
It looks as though in the course of time this definition may be used to assert a claim over these particular areas. We have heard of the claims being made by the province of Newfoundland to certain areas out to sea. This particular clause of Bill C-103 is one which I am sure members from Newfoundland will look at most carefully. The question that must be asked is whether the federal government has decided to insert this clause in order to acquire title by definition in a statute dealing primarily with other matters rather than by proceeding directly by statute to make this claim. I do not know the answer but I believe we should inquire into this matter more thoroughly in the days ahead.
On page 23 of the bill we see a new clause, in two parts, outlining Canadian ownership provisions. This includes a
petroleum ownership charge, which is a levy, and a Canadian ownership account, which is a fund into which the proceeds of that levy are to go. Presumably, future and past acquisitions are financed through that account. For example, there was the purchase of the non-Canadian firm Petrofina. Petrofina was a refining and distribution system which had no petroleum resources-only outlets-but we are expected to believe that through the purchase of outlets the government was contributing toward energy self-sufficiency in this country. I believe it was a highly questionable acquisition because it was obviously done for visibility.
As well, there is the purchase of Pacific Petroleums and Merit, two refiners and distributors in the west which have visible outlets-all displaying white and red signs-and Petrofina in the east with blue and white signs which now have become red and white. Although this is visible evidence of the distribution of products, there is certainly no evidence whatsoever-and therefore no justification for these acquisitions- that they contributed, one drop of petroleum to Canada's selfsufficiency.
It is worth remarking that the bells rang for those 15 days in our favour and for the benefit of Canadians. In Bill C-94, the petroleum ownership charge was to have been as high as $25 per cubic metre, whereas the new bill, C-103, has reduced that levy to $7.25 per cubic metre. That is, from $4 a barrel to $1.15 a barrel, the current rate. Once again the bells won that concession. While other aspects of this bill deserve comment, I think I have exposed enough concerns in order to reach some conclusions.
I do not wish to take up more time of the House because other members wish to speak, but I just repeat that these are some matters which must be kept in mind and considered. I have dealt with these levies separately, remembering that these separate levies should be added to the 60 cents per gallon at the pump which we are now paying the federal government. We are now paying over $2 a barrel for our gasoline. If these extra levies reach their maximum, the cost of regular gasoline will rise from $2 per gallon to $2.96 per gallon. Presumably this is working toward energy self-sufficiency. However, in the process we are importing 300,000 barrels a day and paying $20 million a day for it.
I have not touched upon the issue of home heating oil. The Conservative government had proposed an increase of 18 cents per gallon of gasoline for our cars. We are now faced with a levy of something in the order of 52 cents a gallon, which is almost three and a half times more. With respect to heating oil, our party had made it quite clear that Canadians would be enjoying a heating tax credit. The levy which we have been discussing in this bill will apply just as heavily and onerously to heating oil as it does to automotive oil.
On the strength of that comment I can draw my remarks to a close because I believe the message I wanted to make is now clear. We will be paying almost triple the amount we are now
April 26, 1982

paying for our gas and we will be paying heavily as well for our heating oil. Next winter will be a hard one for those hit with those increases, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to speak to Bill C-103 this afternoon. I carefully listened to the comments of the previous speaker and I share a number of his concerns. Various members of the New Democratic Party have had an opportunity to discuss a number of aspects of Bill C-103, particularly with respect to a number of clauses which we would like to see amended. Since the bill will proceed from this second reading stage into the appropriate committee for intensive study where some amendments will hopefully be made, I would like to take this opportunity to sum up a number of concerns which our party has and conclude this debate on Bill C-103 so that we may debate some other bills which form part of this over-all energy legislation.
When Bill C-103 is reviewed, it can be seen that it is not an energy bill, petroleum administration bill or an energy security bill. Although it is entitled the Energy Administration Act, it is not really that either. It is more like a tax bill and could even be described by some as a desperate tax bill. This bill which deals with the very critical, crucial and strategic energy sector will result in Canadians paying more tax than ever before.
When one considers that the Canadian taxpayer will be the loser, I believe it is a fair question to ask who the winners will be. When one reviews Bill C-103 closely we see, as is the case with other energy bills, that the major winners will be the oil companies operating in Canada, most of which are foreign controlled and owned. Those companies will be the primary beneficiaries of Bill C-103. Those Canadians who will be paying these additional taxes on gas and heating fuels are those who can least afford it. That is why these taxes are regressive. Those are the people today who are on fixed incomes and those who find themselves unemployed or about to be unemployed as a result of the policies of the federal government. Those on fixed pensions or fixed incomes of one kind or another are being pressed to the wall. We do not see legislation coming in which will give an energy tax credit to people in need. We do not see legislation coming in to give some assistance to those people who depend for so much of their livelihood on energy. I am thinking here of the farmers, the food producers of the country, when it comes to Canadians generally.
Perhaps the media is not paying much attention to bill C-103, but the people of Canada certainly should be. However, they have essentially given up in their frustration and anxiety. They have been duped by the federal government. They were duped back in 1980 during the federal election when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went from one end of the country to the other promising Canadians that the price of gasoline would be going down and that the Liberals would not tolerate increases in the prices of gasoline, diesel fuels or heating fuels. A little over two years ago, he promised Canadians that the
Energy Administration Act
Liberals would not tolerate significant increases in these very critical areas. We now know that that was certainly a falsehood and that, indeed, the price is now higher, I suppose, than almost anyone believed possible in two short years.
While prices at the pumps are going up and while prices are going up for home heating fuels, we sit in this House and debate bills which will give billions of dollars in the next handful of years, not to Canadian consumers but, rather, to the oil companies. We are also going out of our way to announce a number of tax concessions, not to Canadians, not to consumers and taxpayers but, rather, to the large oil companies operating in Canada which, as I said earlier, are primarily foreign controlled and foreign owned.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: So they can sell us back our oil.

So they can sell us back the oil that rightfully belongs to us. We wonder why Canadians have essentially given up. We wonder why Canadians feel they have been duped by the federal government. Well, it is perfectly clear. There is certainly no question in our minds in this corner of the House as to why that attitude exists today.
Essentially, this bill can be broken down into six different components. Let me take just a moment or two in which to identify these components, and then 1 want specifically to refer to a number of them. First, Bill C-103 will raise the oil export charge ceiling, will confirm the charges imposed since May, 1979 and will therefore give authority to turn over 50 per cent of the resulting revenue to the producing provinces. That is one of the aspects of Bill C-103. It will establish the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge. It will establish a blended price for oil. It will establish the authority for, and then the termination of, a special compensation charge relating to the cut-off of Alberta oil last year. This legislation will end the Petroleum Compensation Board and allow for the continuation of its work to be done in an expanded way by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It will also establish the Canadian ownership special charge and the Canadian ownership account.
The petroleum compensation charge will be a mechanism whereby the blended price of oil will be developed. It will be charged at the pumps so that all Canadians depending upon gasoline for transportation will pay it. As I say, that is a very regressive way of taxing people. It is intended to compensate refiners who are now forced to import expensive foreign oils while oil wells are capped out in western Canada.
I think the question we must ask is why Canada is not selfsufficient in oil today.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Lack of effort.

We are self-sufficient when it comes to energy per se. However, when it comes to this very strategic energy resource, we are continually dependent upon imports from foreign countries. Why is this? I suspect that when we answer the question we then bring into question the integrity of the major oil companies operating in Canada today. This is

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
because back in the early 1970s we were exporting half our daily production. The oil companies told the federal government that we had enough oil in the ground in reserve to last at least 300 years. Therefore, they asked: "Why not export oil? Why not export half of what we produce on a daily basis?"
If that had been a fact, then perhaps the case could be made. But in 1973, at the outbreak of the OPEC crisis, we had to realign those particular figures, because then the oil companies told us that we did not have enough oil for 300 years; rather, we had enough for only 11 years. They said we needed to get out and explore for new oil and develop new reserves.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: A "minor miscalculation".

As my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) indicates, it was a minor miscalculation-about 280 years out. However, that was because at that time this country depended, and virtually still does today, upon information from the foreign oil companies to enable us to plan for the future. What country in the world would tolerate that? What oil producing country in the world would tolerate being dependent upon foreign producers for its data base? Only Canada, once more leading the world in this rather exotic fashion.
Back in 1973, we found out that we had enough oil for only 11 years. Some of the oil companies came to the federal government and to the Canadian public and said: "We need to explore; but, of course, we will not pay for exploration ourselves as we cannot afford it. Our profits are minimal. Therefore, we need support from the Canadian taxpayers." That is what they are stating today. Hon. members have seen the commercials on television and the newspaper ads stating the concern of the oil companies, such as Gulf and Imperial Oil, for the future oil security of Canada, and that they need support in their exploration for new oil. Bill C-103 will be one more step toward giving the oil companies $6.5 billions to assist them in their exploration.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: We cannot afford it.

We certainly cannot afford $6.5 billion to assist in exploration. We are saying to the oil companies that for every dollar they spend up there in the frontier areas and for every dollar they spend exploring for oil offshore, the Canadian taxpayers will pick up 93 cents of the tax, and that we will ask the companies to pick up 7 cents of the tax. We are saying to the oil companies that if oil is found, however, we want a cut of the action. We want some of the equity as a result of this investment. We are saying that we will invest 93 per cent but that we want 25 per cent equity. Can one imagine any business operator running his or her business under those conditions, 25 per cent of the action for 93 per cent of the risk? Yet that is what we are being asked to support here in the House. It is absolute madness. I suspect that if we are to be paying 93 cents on the dollar for 25 per cent of the action, we should probably add on the extra 7 cents, pay a dollar for a dollar, and get 100 per cent of the action. That would be a much more sound business arrangement.
But we know the scenario. The oil companies need support, so they will ask the taxpayers of Canada to help them out. We will find more oil, we will have a surplus of oil, and we will then be asked to give permission to export oil because of this surplus. We will then find out that our figures were incorrect and that we have another problem. We will find that we need to explore for more petroleum opportunities, the oil companies will come to the Canadian government to ask for more support by the taxpayers, and we will give it. Then there will be a surplus of oil and we will be on the old treadmill all over again.
That is the kind of madness that Canadians are no longer prepared to tolerate. They are no longer prepared to support this kind of mentality. I think the recent Gallup poll very clearly indicates that fact. In a very extensive Gallup poll, Canadians were asked, "Are you interested in having Petro-Canada as the dominant oil industry in this country? Are you interested in self-sufficiency by the year 1985, where more than 75 per cent of the oil industry would be Canadian controlled?" The answer was overwhelmingly yes. Seventy per cent of Canadians said that is what they want. That is why I suspect my friends in the Tory party are not responding very positively to the wishes of Canadian citizens. The taxpayers of Canada want this madness to stop.
Let us talk for a moment or two about the refiners who are receiving these compensation charges because they have presumably been forced to buy at excessive world prices and must therefore be compensated. If you look carefully at the figures, Mr. Speaker, you find that many of the refiners are being overcompensated between $7 and $12 a barrel. In other words, they are not able to buy cheap oil on the spot market of the world and are compensated on the average price of landed oil in the port of Montreal.
In a sense, many of the refineries in central Canada are making money to the tune of $7 to $12 per barrel. When you consider the amount of oil being moved through the central Canadian refineries, it means that some people are making virtually windfall profits. Who is paying for these windfall profits? Who is paying for this illogical compensation payment? Once again it is the taxpayers of Canada. They are paying certain refineries in central Canada more money than they require to compensate for the purchase of foreign oil. Very clearly, we need a more accurate system of calculating this compensation rate. That is one thing we will be advocating and speaking very loudly about when this bill goes to committee.
What is sad for a member of Parliament from western Canada is the fact that we are now shutting in wells in western Canada. This is because the refineries in central Canada are not required to buy western oil. This is being done to the tune of about 30,000 barrels per day of production. Each day 30,000 barrels are locked into the ground as we import expensive foreign oil. Some people say that by the end of the summer it will not be 30,000 but 300,000 barrels per day.
April 26, 1982

That is a tragic situation when you consider the economic problems facing much of the oil industry in western Canada, with special emphasis on the small operators within the industry, the service industries and so on. The big companies are able to take care of themselves, but the small independent entrepreneurs in western Canada are being pushed to the wall. This is because we have a weak federal government that is only asking eastern refiners to give preference to western Canadian oil. If we are going to be locked into this kind of compensation payment, we need to do more than ask the refiners. Indeed, we should require the use of Canadian oil wherever and whenever possible.
The issue is that this whole matter is extremely costly to Canadians. Canadians find it frustrating to know that if they cross the border they can pick up gasoline significantly cheaper than in Canada. While it might appear their prices are going to stabilize or drop a bit, ours are guaranteed to increase. Canadians wonder why they are paying more than they have to in terms of compensation rates to the refiners and why they are paying the oil companies billions of dollars per year. Why are we not prepared to change the tax structure which will result in a more equitable tax flow from the oil companies? These are questions that members opposite have not had the opportunity to respond to.
The present rate of compensation to importers of foreign oil is $17.32 per barrel. Who pays? The consumers of Canada. In 1981-82, compensation charges cost the consumers $5.16 billion in one year. This present year they cost the taxpayers close to $3 billion. It will cost the consumers of Canada $3 billion when it should not be costing them anything. We can and ought to be delivering oil to the eastern refineries, something we would be doing if we had the foresight and planning that this industry requires. The present petroleum compensation charge per barrel of crude Canadian oil is $6.30, again coming from Canadians paying their heating bills.
It is clear that based on the Gallup poll which I referred to earlier, and based on the kinds of charges that are being levied against Canadian consumers and passed along primarily to the oil companies, there is only one way to go. The people of Canada must become a more major player in this critical and strategic industry. The only real way to do that would be through public ownership of a major sector of this industry.
If we are going to pay out $6.5 billion in the next five years to the oil companies, perhaps we ought to ask ourselves what would be the price to buy Imperial oil. How much would it cost Canadian taxpayers to purchase Canadian Imperial Oil? The charge would not be $6.5 billion, but $4.5 billion for the largest oil company operating in this country. That would certainly put us in the driver's seat of this strategic industry. It would go a great distance toward returning to the people of Canada the benefits from this industry.
We do not want to be duped again by the government suggesting that PetroCan is a major player. That is the impression one gets. We know the major player in the oil industry is Imperial Oil. In terms of Canadian owned industry, it is not PetroCan that leads the pack; there are five ahead of it on the
Energy Administration Act
list. Dome Petroleum and others are ahead. When you see the fancy ads and the rhetoric of the federal government regarding PetroCan, Mr. Speaker, you must be very careful.
Dome is Canadian.

I appreciate that. I said that Petro-Canada is not the largest Canadian oil company operating in this country. Dome Petroleum is the largest, and there are other Canadian owned oil companies with it. What is disappointing is that the present government apparently has no plans to make PetroCan the major player in the league.
The Canadian ownership special charge that was intended to provide the capital to purchase oil companies in order to expand the amount of Canadian ownership has been reduced from a possible maximum of $4 per barrel to $1.15 per barrel. That means the takeover money that was supposed to be coming from this special levy simply will not be available. The strategic industry to which this bill is addressed will continue to be dominated by foreign oil companies. Decisions regarding this strategic resource will continue to be made in the board rooms of foreign countries around the world. I cannot imagine why anyone would suggest that is in the best interests of Canada's future.
I want to refer to a couple of critical clauses of this bill that need to be changed. One allows the federal government to set the price of oil in the territories. Time and again the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said that, in his estimation, the concept of federalism is dead in this country. Most members of this House do not feel that way. In fact, federalism is something we want to nurture, encourage and support. The way to do that is not by saying to those who live and govern in the Territories that when it comes to setting the price of oil, we have no faith in them, that we will set the price here in Ottawa because we know what is best for those living in the Northwest Territories and Yukon. It seems to me that a much more positive step, a step that will recognize the concept of federalism that will or ought to exist in this country, is to negotiate a price for oil found in the territories of Canada. This is something that we will be advocating, Mr. Speaker, when the bill gets into committee.
We were very disappointed to find that the draft of Bill C-103 had been altered by the time it got to the House. In the draft it was made very clear that once the pricing arrangements had been made between the federal government and the provincial governments, if there was a difficulty or an impasse, then the federal government would have the final word; they would have paramountcy in this particular matter. In the concept of federalism and recognizing the realities of Canada, we have no difficulty with that; we have to accept it. In the end, if a price has to be determined, we have to accept the responsibility for setting that price.
Nevertheless, in the draft legislation, if a number of members in the House stood up and wanted to debate that issue, so that it became a clearly understood issue in Canada, then that

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
option would be available to them and there would be a debate, although limited in time; but at least, it would be an issue to be placed before the people of Canada. Bill C-103 eliminates that option. The Liberal government is saying: "Listen, we want the opportunity to set this rate arbitrarily or unilaterally, if necessary; we do not want to discuss it in Parliament; we do not want to have even half an hour's debate on it in Parliament". To me, Mr. Speaker, that is undemocratic; it is not operating in the spirit that Canadians have grown to love over the years and it is certainly working against the very principle of a democratic society and parliamentary government.
I am looking forward to getting into committee and asking the members opposite to explain why it is they want to stop debate on such a critical issue, why they will not allow us to debate it, and what made them change their minds on that original draft proposal.
There are some clauses one could identify, Mr. Speaker, but previous speakers in the New Democratic Party have identified the areas of major concern to us. There are some areas we feel are appropriate and there are some steps in the legislation that we feel are good, that need to be taken; but certainly a great deal of fine tuning still remains.
I suppose that my personal disappointment, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to Bill C-103, is that because of the number of points that my colleagues and I have raised, it demontrates very clearly that the people of Canada have lost faith in their political leaders. It demonstrates very clearly why the people of Canada have lost faith in the Liberal government. At a time when every single Canadian is feeling the pinch as a result of high energy prices, whether they be putting diesel fuel in tractors or in boats or simply filling up an automobile at the pump when going to and from work, or paying the heating bills at the end of the month, the people of Canada would like to see a government that has some courage and is prepared to stand up and say: "Enough of this; it is time that we got control of this very strategic industry". It is not like copper; it is not like the cedar industry; ii is not like the apple industry. This particular industry provides the very framework for western culture, for our way of life. It is simply not another resource to deal with; it is the very basis of our western North American Canadian culture.
To permit foreign countries and foreign companies to have the say in how this resource is developed, quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, is almost unbelievable. There is virtually not a single country in the world that is a producer of this strategic resource that would allow this to occur, but we are one. It is amazing how we continue on, by duping the Canadian public, by misleading them in election campaigns, by carrying out extensive advertising campaigns, giving the people the impression that we are rushing headlong into obtaining control over this very strategic industry, when in fact we are not. In this party, Mr. Speaker, we feel that it is our role to speak out against such inappropriate legislation and attempt in whatever way possible to communicate to the people that this particular approach must change.

Mr. Speaker, like other speakers before me, I totally agree that the proposed new title of the bill before us-the Energy Administration Act-is a deceptive misnomer. Although energy and administration are involved, this is really a tax bill; or, indeed, it is a highway robery bill. The word "energy" simply indicates from which source the government plans to reap these taxes; and the word "administration" is simply a more palatable word for unlimited power to spend money.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), when speaking to the bill, made a number of astonishing statements. Perhaps even more astonishing was that he made these statements with a straight face. Even though we are nearly at the end of the month, I had half expected him to conclude his remarks by saying "April Fool"! But he did not, so he was obviously very serious when he said:
Our oil and gas pricing schedule, as created in consultation with the provinces, reflects the sense of realism and fairness which characterizes our energy program.
In no sense whatever is the price Canadians now pay, or will be paying, for their gasoline and oil either realistic or fair. It is abominable. And because it is, I suppose in a twisted way it actually does reflect the government's energy program. So the minister was right in that sense.
The minister went on to say that the government's pricing system has three essential advantages over what was proposed by the previous Progressive Conservative government. Let us examine that statement. The Clark government, on the record, proposed that an additional tax of 18 cents a gallon be levied on gasoline only, not on home heating oil. During the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of his government toured the country promising Canadians- cross their little hearts-that under a Liberal government the tax increase would not exceed 14 cents a gallon.
Mr. Speaker, I know we have to be careful what we say in the Flouse of Commons. We could say that they are "playing with the truth" there. I am reminded, and I believe I mentioned this before, that a great statesman in the British House of Commons once questioned one of the speakers there, mentioned the word "lie" and was made to retract, and justly so. However, he then said: "Mr. Speaker, I will not use that word but I will say that the speaker was guilty of a terminological inexactitude".
I suppose that this statement we are dealing with here was sent around the contry over television and radio and this was why the Prime Minister and the group across the way were returned to office in 1980 because the people believed them. First of all, the people thought that 18 cents a gallon was absolutely horrendous and the idea of 14 cents a gallon looked pretty good. Time and again I have mentioned it to people who are unhappy now and I have said: "It serves you right; you thought 18 cents was a tremendous amount and now you have a much higher tax than that." So Canadians to their sorrow have learned that Liberal promises are not written in stone and always right.
April 26, 1982

Under this government the price of gasoline has risen, as we are all well aware, to almost $2 a gallon. Of this amount nearly $1.35 is siphoned off in taxes by the federal and provincial governments-two-thirds of what we are paying. It is almost in the same category as whisky. I am one who says we can tax alcohol in that form reasonably heavily because it is a luxury pure and simple. Perhaps in some people's minds it is a medicine, but I do not buy that too often!
Through individual taxes provincial governments create their share of the burden, and for that they provide many services, including highways and so forth. However, through its tax grab at various levels the federal governments is the real oppressor and the real culprit.
When praising the federal pricing system the minister said that it ensures that prices rise gradually and predictably so that consumers and the Canadian economy in general are given time to adjust. It has been pretty hard to adjust to these prices in the time given to us. In the short time since this government was returned to office and after the government's promising lower prices, the cost of gasoline and home heating oil has risen rapidly and astronomically. I can assure the minister that not a single vehicle owner or home owner has yet adjusted to the shock, and I do not know if consumers ever will. Now throught this bill the minister and the government are seeking authority to raise these prices even higher.
The minister made much of the fact that the price of crude oil is lower in Canada than elsewhere. One of our speakers-I believe the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre)- pointed out that the Canadian consumer does not use crude oil. Canadians use the products of crude oil, and it is the taxes on those products which are crippling consumers. Perhaps we should be devising some sort of small refinery in each of our homes; then we could buy crude oil and refine it ourselves. That way we could circumvent these terrible taxes.
Don't you believe it!

That is quite right; we should not believe it because the government opposite would tax it even on that basis. As I said before, the taxes already being imposed and the increase being proposed amount to nothing more then highway robbery.
If this bill is passed-and I assume it will be-and the government is allowed to impose on gasoline whatever amount of tax it wishes, there will not be anyone left in the country able to afford to drive or, probably, to heat his home.
In the bill the government is seeking authority for the Canadian ownership special charge to allow it to expand its ownership in the oil and gas industry. This charge, which amounts to four cents a gallon, or jj&OO million a year, is now being used to pay off the purchase of Petrofina. What do the ads say? "It's ours". We certainly paid a price for it because the government bought the company at about four or five times the market value. Anyone who watched the stock market saw the astronomical jump in the price of shares of Petrofina. Someone must have had some inside information. I suppose
Energy Administration Act
some were lucky guessers; it was like the Ouija board! A lot of money was made on that. Many of us are well aware of the controversy still surrounding the purchase of that company.
The government, which should have hung its head in shame at the time of the purchase because of the conditions of the purchase, once again gives an indication through this bill of its contempt for the taxpayer. First, it used tax dollars to buy the company at an inflated price in a questionable deal, and now it wants to soak the taxpayer even more to complete the deal. When the purchase is complete, the government plans to use the money collected through the special charge to finance additional purchases of some other oil companies. Again, I presume the government will pay probably two or three times what those companies are worth. If the method of buying Petrofina is any example, Canadians certainly-and understandably-are very reluctant to give the government any money for future deals of this description.
The government promises that any future purchase would only be undertaken after Parliament has had a chance to debate the matter through-and this is a lovely phrase-a negative resolution procedure. The very phrase is indicative of the nature of this government's backhanded and underhanded regard for Parliament and, by extension, for taxpayers. Under the negative resolution procedure, the time for debate in this House and in the other place is limited to three hours in each chamber. Debate would take place without reference to legislation planned, without spelling out the mandate of the new corporation to be created and without any limits being placed on government. And, in a move undoubtedly unconstitutional, if this House did not approve the move and it was approved in the other place, the government would consider the division as consent and go right ahead with its plans.
Another power play for the government in this bill is the petroleum compensation charge and related spending. The government is now collecting about 24 cents a gallon at the pump, or a total of about $3 billion. Every time a Canadian buys a gallon of gasoline, heating oil or diesel fuel, 24 cents of the price paid per gallon is used to subsidize oil imported from Venezuela, Mexico and other offshore sources. This would be understandable if we had none of our own oil here in Canada, but we do. It has been estimated that because of the government's oil import program, 300,000 barrels of non-subsidized Canadian oil is left in the ground each day. That situation is beyond belief. Canadians are paying up to $20 million a day to import the oil we do not extract from our own sources. And because we are not using our own oil, Canadian companies are losing millions of dollars. Some are reducing their operations and, yes, some are even going bankrupt. This has contributed to unemployment and adds significant stress to an already very troubled economy. The problem does not end there. The government, already deeply in debt, has to borrow funds to pay for oil imports, and this only adds to the nation's economic mess.
Is all this bothering the government? Not at all. In this bill the government wants the authority to raise the compensation

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
charge to $7.5 billion per year without coming to Parliament for approval. This is an outrage.
The government says its underlying goal is to Canadianize our oil and gas industry. Well, if this blundering is the way this government works to achieve that goal, the word "Canadianize" may soon be synonymous with "vaporize". Label it "Canadian" and see it vanish!
The transportation fuel recovery charge is yet another form of tax contained in this bill. The government is imposing a special tax on diesel fuel used by Canadian ships engaged in international trade. If the National Energy Program was devised as a means of helping Canadians, why in the world is the government imposing a tax on fuel for Canadian ships which will raise the cost well above prevailing United States prices? The National Energy Program is a prize, all right-a booby prize!
The situation with respect to airline fuel tax is even stranger. The tax on international flights was withdrawn when it was found to be in violation of international agreements but, because the government had already collected the tax, through the bill it seeks authority to legalize the collection of that illegal tax. This is an amazing situation, one which clearly illustrates how this government operates.
Returning to the petroleum compensation charge for a moment, a method of operation this government frequently employs, the compensation charge was originally established to create a special fund to subsidize Syncrude production to domestic levels. To keep Canadian prices down we were prepared to pay producers for their loss, and the charge was to cover the subsidy. The charge was not considered a tax; it was money being collected for a special fund. However, when the federal government chose to try to bring the government of Alberta to heel and began importing costly offshore oil, the minister, through a ways and means motion, raised the price of the compensation charge. The legality of this method of increasing the charge was in dispute, but the government paid no attention.
Now, through this bill, it again seeks to legalize and expand on an illegal act. Accountability, like Canadianization, is a word whose meaning has been drastically altered under this government. In matters of energy, as indeed in many other areas affecting the lives of Canadians, the government has promised the moon and delivered instead a black hole. What matters to the people has become anti-matter to the government. Perhaps scientists seeking to make contact with alien life forms would do well to focus their efforts and attention on the other side of the House. The government, in the street vernacular, is doing its own thing, in its own space. The people of Canada should unite in an instant to send the government and this bill into a more appropriate place-into space.
As we are all well aware, the bill is going to legitimize taxes which the government has been collecting illegally. As I mentioned before, I believe that out of every dollar the consumer pays for gasoline, 30 cents goes to the producer, the
service station and others and 70 cents goes to the provincial and federal governments.The federal government takes the lion's share and now it is going to avail itself, through this bill, of the opportunity to take more.
I think that most Canadians are aware of the bell ringing that went on for two weeks. There was some criticism of this party by certain people in the country but not the majority. The calls and letters that I received from my riding and adjacent riding, which is held by a Liberal cabinet minister, were from people who were screaming blue murder or patting us on the back. They were telling us to keep it up and show the government that it cannot be as autocratic and dictatorial as it wants to be. The ringing of the bells saved the taxpayers of Canada a sizeable amount of money.
Rubbish! Absolute nonsense!

Prove it. Read the bill. That monstrosity, Bill C-94, with about 148 pages, would have empowered the government to collect up to 98 cents per gallon of gasoline. At least now the government has agreed to reduce that to 52 cents per gallon. There is no question that this party made a worthwhile effort on behalf of the Canadian people. The majority of the people are now wringing their hands and asking why they ever believed the government when it was running around at election time saying it was going to keep the price of energy down below the 18 cents per gallon that the Conservative government had advocated.

Mr. Speaker, occasionally in this House there is some value in repetition. Today all Canadians have the right to ask if Liberal members of Parliament will vote for the 52 cents per gallon tax on gasoline. They were elected because they told Canadians that 18 cents per gallon was too much. Will they vote today for a tax of 52 cents per gallon on gasoline? That is the question.

Today, all Canadians have the right to ask if Liberal members will vote for an increase in the tax on gasoline, of 52 cents a gallon and not 18 cents.

Today all Canadians have the right to ask if Liberal members of Parliament will vote for a 52 cents per gallon tax on gasoline. They were elected because they told Canadians that 18 cents per gallon was too much. Will they vote today for a tax of 52 cents per gallon on gasoline?

Today, all Canadians have the right to ask if Liberal members are going to vote for an increase in the tax on gasoline of 52 cents, not 18 cents per gallon, but 52 cents per gallon.

Today all Canadians have the right and the obligation to ask if the Liberal members will vote for an increase in gasoline tax of 52 cents per gallon. They told Canadians that they were elected because they said 18 cents per gallon was too much.
April 26, 1982

Today, will the Liberals stand up in this House and vote for an increase in gasoline taxes of 52 cents per gallon?

Today, everyone in the province of Quebec has the right to ask if Liberal members are going to vote for an increase in the tax on gasoline of 52 cents a gallon, not 18 cents, but 52 cents a gallon.

It is too bad that every television set in the nation will not be tuned in for the vote today. All Canadians have the right to watch Liberal members of Parliament. Will they stand up in the House today, and at report stage and at third reading stage, and vote to increase the gasoline tax by 52 cents per gallon when they won an election claiming that 18 cents a gallon was too much? Will they stand up in the House and vote for a tax increase of 52 cents per gallon? All Canadians have the right to watch and listen and look at their behaviour.

Today, all Canadians, and everyone in the province of Quebec have the right to ask if Liberal members are going to vote for an increase in the tax on gasoline of 52 cents, not 18 cents per gallon.

Today in this House, as the day goes by, as we get closer to the vote, we are going to witness one of the most hypocritical actions ever perpetrated on the Canadian people when members of the Liberal party stand in the House and vote for an increase in gasoline taxes of 52 cents per gallon. They went to the Canadian people and said that 18 cents was too much. Was 18 cents too much?
