speechtext: Go on to the next paragraph.

Did the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin) stand on a platform and tell his electors that 18 cents per gallon was too much? Is the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie going to stand in the House today and vote for an increase of 52 cents per gallon? How is the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie going to explain that to his voters?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Go back to your French for a little variation.

A little French, says the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, for a little variation.

Are the Liberal members from Quebec today going to vote for a tax increase? An increase that is not going to be 18 cents but 52 cents per gallon, and that is the truth.
Later today all of those members from Quebec will stand in this House and vote for one simple tax, 52 cents a gallon. Before the bells rang it was 98 cents a gallon, and I hope Canadian taxpayers understand that 16 days of bell ringing saved them 46 cents a gallon. I hope Canadians understand that the Liberal Party of Canada later today will drive the final nail into the coffin of their integrity. When they stand in
Energy Administration Act
this House and vote for a single tax which will increase the price of gasoline 52 cents a gallon after promising the electors to keep it below 18 cents a gallon, their integrity goes out the window. Win an election, break your promise, and look at yourself in the mirror each morning. Ask yourself about your own personal sense of integrity. Is that what politics in Canada is all about?
I could stay on that theme, Mr. Speaker, and in some ways I would like to stay on that theme, for whatever time is allowed me, because that is the fundamental principle in Bill C-103. The integrity of democracy is being challenged by this legislation. It is not right or good for our democracy when politicians go on public platforms and make clear and consistent statements to the voters about their intentions, and then go back on their promises when they win the election. Repeated behaviour of that kind undermines the integrity of the democratic process. It makes each and every Canadian less willing to cooperate with their government. It makes the continuation of our democracy less certain in the long term. It is that kind of behaviour which lies at the heart of the feelings of alienation in western Canada, and it lies at the heart of a growing and strengthening separatist movement. If you cannot trust your government, if we do not have a system which holds politicians responsible for their promises, then the integrity of the people who live in that region of the country will produce a political system which they can trust.
As 1 sat in committee with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) the other day, I was bitterly and deeply disappointed at his lack of comprehension of that fact. As I stand here today to debate Bill C-103,1 do so with a sense of sadness about a National Energy Program which has been an absolute unmitigated disaster for all Canadians. Not just Canadians who live in the west, but all Canadians.
We have a government which said it would keep the price of Canadian oil at a level which would never exceed 75 per cent of the world price. If you are a lawyer and read the fine print, Mr. Speaker, you might be able to argue that that promise has been kept. But if you just apply a little common sense, you know it has not. The application of that common sense begins by simply getting into your car anywhere in Canada and driving south across the American border, going to the nearest service station and buying gasoline. American gasoline is sold at world price and it is cheaper than Canadian gasoline. The minister and other Liberal members of Parliament will stand up on public platforms and say they kept our price at 75 per cent of world price, yet gasoline is more expensive in Canada than it is in the United States.
How can that be, Mr. Speaker? The simple explanation is that two-thirds of what we pay is taxes, one-third is for the gasoline. The price of gasoline in Canada is about $2 a gallon; if all taxes were dropped then the consumer could buy gasoline for somewhere between 65 and 70 cents a gallon. That is the reality of the NEP. The Liberal party was elected in February, 1980 and gasoline was about $1 a gallon; today it is $2. The price has doubled and the difference, Mr. Speaker, is taxes.

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
What else have they accomplished? Seventeen billion dollars has left Canada since the introduction of the NEP. Think of that! Seventeen billion dollars which could have been used to create jobs for Canadians, to keep our interest rates down and to build hospitals! The NEP has chased $17 billion out of this country. It has chased out of Canada almost half the drilling rigs, the trucks, tractors and diesel engines, all of the equipment which is needed to drill an oil well. Is it surprising, Mr. Speaker, to find that these people left with their money and equipment?
In October, 1980, we had probably the finest pool of trained talent in that industry which existed anywhere in the world. Then because of an ill considered policy and a minister who does not know what he is doing, we have chased these trained people, equipment and jobs out of this country. This nation is poorer because of it, and our unemployment rolls are growing daily.
Never in the history of this nation has an individual been so misguided and so harmful to our nation than the current Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. What is so tragic is that so many Liberal members of Parliament have had faith in his judgment and in his statistics when they should not have. But as a consequence of that misplaced faith, their constituents are suffering.
I want to give Liberal members of Parliament an example of the consequences of that misplaced faith. One of the taxes to be found in Bill C-103 is the 48-cent a gallon levy for the petroleum compensation charge. For members of Parliament who want an explanation of some of the 12 ways in which taxpayers' money is wasted through that charge, I invite them to read the April 6 transcript of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. There are two sets of minutes for the two meetings which preceded the one of April 6 if hon. members really want to comprehend the background. By reading those minutes, hon. members will find out that in 1978 the compensation charge, which the government sought and which it obtained from Parliament, was at the rate of $1 per barrel. That was four years ago. If hon. members look at the bill that is before us today they will find that the government wants the authority to charge $12 per barrel. That is a 1,200 per cent increase in taxes in four years. It makes our inflation rate at 11 per cent or 12 per cent look insignificant when one realizes that the government itself wants to increase the tax rate 1,200 per cent over a four-year period of time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What about the increase in the heritage fund and the gas profits?
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie would like a diversion. He would like a lecture on the Alberta heritage fund.
What is the government doing with its tax grab?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is being used for health services.

Today, of a $30 charge for a tank full of gas, the federal government takes $10. On average, for every tank full of gas sold throughout Canada, the Alberta government gets about $2. The money is used for hospitals, for education and for the training of people. But in Alberta we understand one simple fact-and we have done so since our province began. If you are going to do a good job of helping those who cannot help themselves, for instance, our senior citizens and the handicapped, first you have to have some income. Therefore, to raise money to help those in need income has to be generated. A sane and sensible public policy begins with that understanding. You cannot help anybody if you do not have the resources, the people or the facilities. There has to be a healthy economy in order to help those who need help.
The oil import compensation charge will be written up by historians as a classic mistake in government policy. The charge today is about $6.30 a barrel, which translates into 24 cents on every gallon of gasoline. It is a flat rate. The tax is the same on a barrel of light crude as on a barrel of heavy crude. How many people in this chamber, and I wonder especially how many Liberal members of Parliament, know that in Alberta alone there are 81 grades of crude, each priced differently. The light crudes are more expensive; the heavy crudes are cheaper. The reason for that is that a barrel of light crude will produce more gasoline and more aromatics, which are used in the plastics industry, and less asphalt. A barrel of heavy crude works in the opposite fashion. Aromatics and gasoline are worth more in the marketplace; asphalt is worth less. But when a flat rate tax is imposed on a barrel of crude, regardless of its quality, its value on the marketplace is distorted, and it is distorted very badly. All of a sudden, the heavy crudes are not competitive with the light crudes. It is an interesting fact that the heavy crudes require more money, more equipment and more people.
When that oil compensation charge is imposed, Canadian jobs are lost to the benefit of foreign imports. We told hon. members opposite about that but they did not believe us. The facts today indicate that we were right. An NDP member mentioned that 30,000 barrels of oil a day are shut in, but the figure is closer to 350,000 barrels a day, quickly rising to 450,000 barrels a day. That shut-in crude is of all grades, but it is the heavy oil, the low quality oil-the employment kind of oil-that is the most frequently shut in. That is partly as a result of the oil import compensation charge.
If hon. members would refer to the evidence before the Public Accounts Committee hearing in early April, hon. members would find that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources also proposed a flat rate compensation principle. A great deal of the oil that is imported from Mexico is called Mayan crude. When a barrel of Mayan crude is brought into Canada, the oil company receives a subsidy from tax dollars of $17.30 a barrel. When that amount is deducted from what is actually paid for the Mayan crude, hon. members will find the refiner, whether it is Imperial Oil or Petro-Canada in Montreal, can buy Mexican crude at 40 per cent less than what Canadian crude of equivalent quality would cost.
April 26, 1982

The government is using your tax dollars and mine, Mr. Speaker, to encourage oil companies to buy crude oil from Mexico, Venezuela and Nigeria, while leaving Canadian oil in the ground and Canadians out of work. If the oil is not pumped and no one is searching for it, who will buy cars and trucks?
When we stop and think about the petroleum compensation fund and put it in our own context, how would tobacco growers in the Niagara Peninsula, for example, feel if the federal government said that it would put a tax on their tobacco, that it would collect the money and give it to tobacco growers from Virginia? How would they feel if the federal government said that it would tax their tobacco and give the money to American tobacco growers, so that their tobacco could be sold in Canada at a price lower than tobacco grown in Canada? How would they feel if the government said that they could leave their tobacco in the sheds to rot?
On the other side, how would Canadian car manufacturers feel if the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) came forward and said that the government would put a tax on all cars produced in Canada amounting to $2,000 per car? How would they feel if the government said that it would take the money and give it to dealers who import Volvos and cars from Britain and Italy, so that foreign cars will cost consumers less than Canadians cars? Would hon. members opposite rise and vote for such a piece of legislation affecting tobacco farmers or car manufacturers? What if it were done with the shoe industry? The government could put a special tax on Canadian made shoes and make them more expensive. It could take the proceeds and give them to those who import shoes from Italy or Spain, which would make Italian and Spanish shoes cheaper than Canadian ones. How many hon. members opposite would rise to support the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on such a policy? Yet this is what they intend to do some time this day with Canadian produced oil. They will rise in the House and support the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on a piece of legislation which has that principle built into it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Explain why the oil companies are buying offshore steel.

The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie might be interested in knowing that oil companies in Canada are laying off staff across the nation. Also he might be interested in knowing that they are not buying pipe from the steel mills in Hamilton or cars from the manufacturing centre in Windsor. They are not buying diesel engines, fan belts or spark plugs because they are reducing the size of their staff and their activities. They have taken their money and put it in the United States. They are buying fan belts, spark plugs, cars and trucks in the United States of America. In Canada we are buying oil from Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico. We are buying lots of it because the federal government in its wisdom decided to tax Canadians from coast to coast. It decided to take the money and make the oil from Mexico, Venezuela and
Energy Administration Act
so on cheaper than Canadian oil, so that oil companies will buy abroad and consumers will pay the price. If hon. members opposite would vote for such legislation in terms of tobacco farmers, shoe manufacturers or automobile manufacturers, then they should rise in the House and vote for it on the oil side as well. But if they would not, they should think twice about standing in the House and voting in such a way when it comes to the commodity called oil.
I heard much talk by members of the New Democratic Party today about public ownership of the oil and gas industry, not private ownership. I should like to talk about hospitals and medical care and public ownership. When hon. members of the NDP rise in the House or in committee and say that $5.5 billion for Petro-Canada is not enough, then Canadians should be asked whether they want their tax dollars used to buy service stations or hospital beds. That is the reality of the choice. If they seek permission to tax, then they should have the courage to lay out the choices for spending. The choice which the Liberal government is making, and the choice which the NDP is supporting, is to take tax dollars from Canadians to buy service stations rather than hospital beds. Anyone who reads the daily newspapers will know that the medical system in the country is facing day by day an increasing sense of crisis. The trained people who make it go-the nurses, the doctors and the technicians-are unhappy because the amount of money for the system is inadequate. But Liberal members rose and voted to cut $5.7 billion worth of spending for that purpose; they stood the other day in the House and said: "Take that money and give it to the board of directors of Petro-Canada to buy service stations and oil wells". They have not asked Canadians if that is the choice they would like the government to make. Do Canadians want to be taxed to buy service stations or to provide medical care? That is the essence of the choice.
The NDP want the ownership charge in the bill to be used to make Petro-Canada larger and larger, but the reality is that the exploration end of the oil and gas industry requires money, people and equipment. All those commodities are in short supply in the world, but all those commodities in the industry are movable. Money and trained people can move to any nation; the equipment is mobile and it can be moved to any nation. It is not a great deal different in the health care system. The equipment is stationary but the trained people can move. They can want Petro-Canada to be as big as they want, they can take money from Canadians in the form of taxation and put money into it, but they are wasting money unless people will work for the company. We are not talking about untrained people. We are talking about geophysicists, tool pushers and people who have spent years obtaining the necessary experience to perform in the industry. When they are in short supply around the world, they choose to work for private sector companies. If we put our money into Petro-Canada we will not be able to hire enough skilled people; we will waste our dollars on unskilled people.

Energy Administration Act

When we remove that money from our health care system, we will lose our trained medical people; they will leave Canada to go to other countries. At the same time as we will have an inefficient and costly oil and gas industry which will not work, we will have created an unworkable health care system. That is the nature of these Liberal government policies which it has proposed over and over again in the House. It is time for the government to begin thinking and learning. It is time for those Liberal members to tell the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to come to his senses before it is too late.

Mr. Speaker, it never ceases to amaze me when I listen to debates in the House to see how quickly times change. It was only a year ago that we heard members opposite asking us why we were not raising our oil prices to world levels in order to commence development and to achieve an agreement with Alberta. Now that they recognize that we have an agreement which was made after more than a year of negotiations-an agreement which the Conservatives were not able to arrive at-they are the first to criticize it. They are criticizing an agreement which is not
only a benefit to the petroleum industry but to Canada as a whole.
The Conservative party wants to know what we are doing with the taxes which were raised as a result of that agreement. I should explain initially that 67 per cent of the cost of hospitalization insurance comes from federal coffers. The government provided for 59 per cent of medicare and 35 per cent of extended health care, and when you consider that in Ontario the federal government pays part of the cost of Grade 13 in the secondary schools and research in the universities, the amount rises to more than 62 per cent.
The government pays 50 per cent of the cost of crop insurance; the other 50 per cent is paid by the producers themselves while the provinces administer this plan. The government pays 50 per cent of the cost under the Canada Assistance Plan. Is the Conservative party suggesting that we should do away with these programs? Do they suggest, as one member did this afternoon, that the provinces should build the highways and make all the material improvements and that the federal government should neglect the welfare of Canadians? Should we neglect our senior citizens who helped build this country?
I feel I must comment on a point which was made about gasoline prices being cheaper in some areas of the United States than in Canada. The Conservatives conveniently forget to point out that our dollar is valued at approximately 18 cents below the American dollar and that the American gallon is approximately 20 per cent less than ours. Conservatives members forget to mention these facts when making their speeches.
Another assertion made by Conservative members is that Canadian drilling rigs have moved south. However, these rigs began to leave in September of 1981, before the National Energy Program was announced. The reason they moved south was that we had literally thousands of gas wells in western Canada shut-in with no markets or pipelines to hook on to those wells. As a matter of fact, there are gas wells in my own constituency which were discovered in 1977 and only this year have they been able to be hooked up to the main transmission lines which are less than five miles away.
When the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) spoke in this debate on April 22, he made reference to fertilizer and the fact that the price of natural gas has a direct impact on the price of fertilizer. I should remind him that fertilizer prices this spring, especially in my area, are less than they were a year ago. Prices a year ago, as indicated in one particular analysis, were $250 per tonne; at 8-32-16. Those various components reflect the percentage of nitrogen, phosphorous and potash in each tonne. That particular analysis a year ago was $250 cash per tonne, picked up at the local warehouse. This year I have received quotes of $236 per tonne. Today, nitrogen prills containing 45 per cent urea costs $296 per tonne. Our invoices show that we paid $310 per tonne a year ago. These certainly are not increases by any stretch of the
April 26, 1982

imagination. They are, rather, adjustments in the price reflecting the demand and supply situation in Canada and reflecting the surplus of many raw material products which we have.
The hon. member for Vegreville also mentioned that these products could be bought cheaper in the United States. He indicated that it was $30 to $60 per tonne less in the United States. I must remind him that the currency exchange for that particular analysis priced at $236 per tonne which 1 mentioned earlier would amount to $47 per tonne on exchange alone. Obviously, it would be cheaper in the United States.
I would also point out that the federal government does not set retail prices of gasoline or diesel fuel. The federal government establishes the price paid by refiners for their crude, and it should also be borne in mind that the federal government has no jurisdiction over resources in a province but only over interprovincial and international trade.
The blended price at the beginning of this year is 70.6 per cent of the world price. The old price was 54.4 per cent of world price. The newly discovered oil, tar sands oil and imported oil are blended with that old price to arrive at the blended price. This is a price which we negotiated for more than two years and it is one in which we intend to continue.
When we compare our price per barrel, it is still lower than that which was proposed by the opposition. We are still lower in our wellhead natural gas price than the opposition would have been had they continued with their proposed price structure as contained in their 1979 budget.
We achieved an agreement with the provinces whereby the percentage share for the Government of Canada rose from 11 per cent to 25.5 per cent. The province receives slightly over 30 per cent while the oil companies get 44.3 per cent of the wellhead price. Certainly this is an achievement. Our government recognized that we were faced with an oil and gas industry which was very heavily foreign owned and controlled at the end of 1980. Fully 72 per cent of oil and gas revenues ultimately accrued to foreign owned companies or foreigners. Furthermore, 78 per cent of these revenues were accounted for by foreign controlled companies in Canada. This compares to a level of 52 per cent in the United Kingdom and 10 per cent to 15 per cent in the United States.
There have been many comments with respect to the present level of the petroleum compensation charge. I would remind hon. members opposite that one year ago the Alberta government was cutting production. This necessitated the rise in the petroleum compensation charge. Now, at a time when the market demand has slowed, the Conservatives are complaining about the cutbacks. Not only is the level of foreign ownership and control very high but a review of the major oil industry competitors clearly indicates the dominance of foreign companies in Canada's oil industry. Eleven of the 15 largest oil and gas producers are foreign owned and controlled, with the top eight positions being held by foreign companies. Not only was the domination of foreign companies pervasive, but it seemed likely that the situation would become almost worse.
Energy Administration Act
Future major oil supply in Canada would not be from traditional sources in the western Canadian basin but, rather, oil supplies would be increasingly diverted from massive oil sands plants on exploration sites in the Arctic and on lands well offshore. These future sources of energy supply required vast sums of money and a great deal of technical know-how. Foreign companies were, and in many cases still are, in the best position to take advantage of these future opportunities. However, it is only with the participation of the Government of Canada, along with that of the provinces, that development of our resources can continue, particularly in the area of the heavy tar sands, where we see that the companies are backing off, not because of any actions by either the provincial or federal levels of government, but because of the glut of oil on the world markets and because the return that they expect from their money is not there.
Given this situation, the following questions must be asked: What government in the developed world would tolerate the large degree of foreign participation in an industry as significant as we have here in Canada? Have we Canadians an obligation to ensure that this industry stays under Canadian control?
Where were you when they asked you for help in the first place?

I submit that we have an obligation and that this bill provides the basis of fulfilling that obligation. Certainly, what government would have allowed such dominance in its strategic industry which, in Canada's case, is responsible for about 10 per cent of the country's gross national product?
These are the types of questions which the Canadian government had to face in relation to its own economy in the fall of 1980. Its response to the Canadianization objectives and policies was embodied in the National Energy Program of October, 1980. The government stated that it believed that:
-a larger national public sector presence in oil and gas is the only equitable way to meet quickly our goal of increased Canadian ownership. Judging from the results achieved to date by Petro-Canada, it is also an effective way of encouraging the rapid energy development necessary to meet our security needs.
For these reasons, the Government of Canada intends to acquire several of the large oil and gas firms.
This would ensure that the firms stay within the control of the Canadian people, which would be in their best interests. The National Energy Program also stated:
In adopting a program of enlarging the public sector, the government is anxious to ensure that the program is self-financing, and imposes no additional burden on general government revenues. Therefore, the government will establish a Canadian Ownership Account, to be financed by special charges on all oil and gas consumption in Canada, to be used solely to Finance an increase of public ownership in the energy sector. The charges will be set at levels that make this program totally self-financing. The actual rates and the dates of implementation will be determined by the progress of the acquisition program. The charges will be kept at moderate levels in the early years, to limit the impact on consumers.
While the Goverment of Canada is determined to increase Canadian ownership and control, it does not wish the result to be increased concentration of power in the hands of a few large Canadian companies. Competition is the

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
lifeblood of the industry, and the consumer's best protection. A concentrated Canadian industry is an unsatisfactory replacement for a concentrated foreign-owned industry. The intent of the program is to increase the number of Canadian participants. Therefore, the government will be vigilant about ownership trends in the industry. The Petroleum Monitoring Agency will play a key role, through its function of advising Parliament on the size, financial position and ownership of the oil companies.
In slightly more than a year since the announcement of the National Energy Program, great strides have been made toward Canadianization. The eighth, fourteenth and eighteenth largest oil and gas companies have been switched from foreign to Canadian control. The level of Canadian ownership, measured by upstream production revenues, has increased by over 6 per cent as a result of some $7.5 billion in mostly private sector acquisitions. We have been able to make this achievement. Petro-Canada, the nationally-owned oil company, now has refining and marketing facilities across Canada, after its recent acquisition of Petrofina which, incidentally, will be paid for later this year.
While we are generally pleased with the progress to date, we realize that there is a great deal yet to be accomplished. It is for this reason that we are proposing the establishment of a Canadian ownership charge and Canadian ownership account. The Canadian ownership special charges, used initially to help finance Petro-Canada's acquisition of Petrofina, would provide for a special charge on domestic petroleum received for processing or consumption in Canada, and foreign petroleum and petroleum products imported into Canada. The charge is currently $7.25 per cubic metre, or approximately $1.16 per barrel, which is the ceiling set by this bill. No greater increases are even authorized by this legislation.
The Canadian ownership special charges would also provide for special taxes increasing the natural gas and gas liquids tax, which is a tax on marketable natural gas, propane, ethane and butane. Increases on the natural gas tax are now 14 cents per gigajoule. Increases on the tax on propane, ethane and butane are $3.55, $2.60 and $3.95 per cubic metre respectively. These amounts are the ceilings set in the bill for the increases. They will not be applied to exports of natural gas or gas liquids. No further increases are authorized by this legislation.
I should also like to point out that under the incremental oil revenue tax, an agreement was reached with the provinces last January which decreases the tax paid by smaller producing wells by 5 per cent for every barrel less than 20 barrels per day. Therefore, a small, very shallow stripper well which produces one barrel per day would, in effect, pay a 5 per cent incremental oil revenue tax. This has a tremendous impact in putting drilling rigs back to work in Alberta, where approximately 40 per cent of the wells fall into this category and account for approximately 10 per cent of the production.
In addition to that, the petroleum gas revenue tax, as raised earlier in the year, is the really ineffective tax of 12 per cent, a reduction from the 16 per cent, a reduction related to a resource allowance. However, in the future, the use of any funds from the Canadian ownership account for other acquisitions would have to be authorized by the governor in council, acting on the recommendation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance. Such uses will be subject to a negative resolution of Parliament.
However, it should be made clear that the direction of the Canadianization thrust has been toward the mobilization of predominantly private Canadian investment by existing companies, pension plans, insurance funds and from individuals. To a great extent, this policy has succeeded since all but one of a dozen acquisitions to date have been by private companies. I should make a small correction, because the Ontario government took part in the acquisition of a private company when it bought 25 per cent control of Suncor. Therefore, really all but two of the acquisitions to date have been by private companies. Furthermore, the federal government is acting as a catalyst for the establishment of a cooperative energy corporation which will bring into the oil and gas sector the savings of millions of Canadian co-op members.
A misconception which we have heard, particularly from abroad, is that the government is creating an unattractive environment for foreign firms which will reduce the value of these firms, allowing them to be purchased at "fire sale" prices. This is an absurd allegation. Canadian companies have paid prices well above market value for foreign-owned assets. Furthermore, foreign-owned oil and gas subsidiaries trading on Canadian exchanges have done no worse than their Canadian-owned counterparts.
Another misconception was the belief that Canadianization policies for the energy sector will be applied in other sectors of the economy, specifically, in the minerals sector. The government has already stated that this will not be the case, and the evidence on the difference in the foreign ownership and control situation in the two industries is a major reason for the difference in policies.
Finally, the objective of Canadianization does not mean that foreign investment and ownership in the oil and gas business is no longer wanted in Canada. Canada is well known for its exciting geological potential. The combined financial and fiscal incentive package offered by the government makes Canada one of the most attractive countries in which to invest. For example, a foreign investor operating in the north or offshore will, after tax deductions and incentive payments, be spending only 53 cents of every exploration dollar.
In fact, a recent comparison made by Petro-Canada of rates of return expected by a foreign investor from a representative pool of new oil shows the following: Canada lands 27.7 per cent, United Kingdom 24.4 per cent, United States 21.6 per cent and Norway 18.3 per cent. I repeat, these calculations are for foreign investors. The figures show that we have created an environment which, when compared to other locations, will be attractive for foreign investors. The government welcomes their participation and asks only that they take into account the legitimate aspirations of Canadian investors and other Canadians to own a share of this vital sector and to exercise some control over decision-making in their own petroleum industry.
April 26, 1982

This view is widely supported by the vast majority of Canadians. Indeed, it is one of the most popular programs established by the Canadian government in many years. The results of a poll done by the Canadian Petroleum Association last year indicates that 84 per cent favour the government's move to make the oil and gas industry in Canada at least 50 per cent Canadian owned. This is a remarkable figure. It indicates the desire and the determination of Canadians to achieve that control so that we are no longer at the mercy of the foreign-owned companies.
With respect to the Canadian ownership special charge, I would like to mention the significant change that was made to these provisions as they appeared in Bill C-94. The legislative authority that appeared in Bill C-94 to raise the Canadian ownership special charge above the present level has been removed. Under the new amendments, the existing Canadiani-zation charge can be decreased but not increased beyond that level by order in council.
The change is as follows. The ceiling on the Canadian ownership special charge on petroleum has been lowered from $25 to $7.25 per cubic metre. The ceiling on increases to the excise tas on natural gas has been lowered from 60 cents to 14 cents per gigajoule, and the ceiling on increases to the excise tax on natural gas liquids has been lowered from $17 per cubic metre to $2.60, $3.55 and $3.95 on ethane, propane and butane respectively.
I would like to leave hon. members with one thought. The government believes that it has created a framework which will both allow significant participation by Canadians in their own oil and gas industry and encourage continued active involvement of those foreign companies which have contributed to the development of this important industry. I am confident that this can be done.
In closing, it should be very clear that in its program to date the Government of Canada has shown it has a flexibility to negotiate, compromise and arrive at an agreement with the oil-producing provinces of this country. It is willing to negotiate with the oil-producing wells to ensure that the incremental oil revenue tax is not an overbearing burden and will not make the production of oil from such wells uneconomic. It has shown the flexibility to make adjustments in many areas. I am confident that as the world energy scene changes, the minister and this government will adapt to those changes in a way that is beneficial, not only to all Canadians and the provinces, but to the industry as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us seeks to amend a 1975 act of Parliament which imposed a charge on exports of crude oil and petroleum products to raise revenue to support the one-price oil policy, which I feel was a good policy, and to attain energy goals.
The measure now before us legalizes the petroleum compensation charge which is currently levied at $6.30 a barrel and which has resulted in an increase in the price of gasoline at the pumps by about 24 cent a gallon. About $1 a barrel or four cents a gallon of that amount has received legal authority. In this bill, the government seeks to give itself the right to
Energy Administration Act
increase the tax to $12 a barrel, or another 24 cents a gallon at the pump.
The second major tax contemplated in the bill is the Canadian ownership charge. It was instituted to raise money to enable Petro-Canada to purchase Petrofina. In this case the levy is $ 1.15 a barrel or about four cents a gallon at the pump.
Since February, 1980 we have experienced a 99-cent increase in the price of a gallon of gasoline, of which 60 cents is directly attributable to federal energy taxes. Home heating oil, which incidentally was exempted from the Crosbie 18-cent a gallon tax, has increased about 66 cents and, while there are undoubtedly other factors involved, the principal thrust of this increase is federal taxes.
As we all know, during the past year there has been a world overproduction of oil and this has caused world prices to fall sharply. The taxes which the government has been adding to the price of gasoline at the pumps during the past two years is supposed to pay for the increasing subsidy the government has been paying on the one-fifth of our oil requirements which could not be supplied by Canadian sources and which must be bought offshore, generally supplying the oil needs of eastern Canada.
The subsidy was necessary so that all Canadians could enjoy the Canadian price. However, if the cost of foreign oil we are subsidizing is falling, the taxes needed to pay for the subsidy should also be decreasing, not increasing. In other words, the price we pay for gasoline at the pump should be coming down, as it has been doing in the United States and in most other countries, not going up.
Indeed, at many points along the Canadian-American border the price of gasoline charged at the pumps in the United States is lower. In many cases so is home heating oil. I suggest that the difference in the value of the dollar does not fully compensate for the magnitude of this difference. The Americans significantly are paying the world price, and I have to ask what we are paying. Increasing energy costs are percolating through our economy, causing serious dislocations.
The inflation rate has risen from 9.3 per cent in March, 1980 to 11.6 per cent in March, 1982. In the past year alone, fuel oil costs have risen by 29.6 per cent, transportation costs by 16.4 per cent, fresh fruit by 28.7 per cent, processed vegetables by 18.8 per cent, communications by 18.7 per cent and owned accommodation by 16.6 per cent.
The purchasing power of the 1971 dollar in March, 1982 was 39 cents. In the past 11 years, the consumer price index has risen by 156 per cent. Food prices have risen by 204 per cent and housing costs by 148 per cent. The 1981 average annual inflation rate of 12.5 per cent was the highest in 33 years. Wages are not keeping pace with inflation. The average wage earner in Canada has lost $285 in annual purchasing power since the February, 1980 election and $635 since the fall of 1977. As we have all been reminded by recent events, short periods of time can cause great changes in political fortunes and in political perceptions. This bill reminds me that just over

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
26 months ago the Liberal party was elected nationally on the platform that higher energy prices were unnecessary and that they could manage the economy better than the Clark government.
Now, 99 cents a gallon later, people are beginning to recall that during the term of office of the Clark government, inflation remained stable, jobs were being created at the rate of 30,000 a month, and the purchasing power of wages rose. Under the self-proclaimed economic miracle workers now in office, we have seen 33-year record levels of unemployment and inflation, declining real wages, the biggest tax burden since the war, the gutting of the passenger rail system, and proposals to reduce the financial commitment to equalizaton, health and post-secondary education.
The 18-cent election issue has come home to roost and it is costing Canadians their economic well-being.
Hear, hear!
