speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-103, which is now before the House, is a piece of legislation about which I would like to say a few words. I address my remarks today particularly to the question of oil export charges, this being the subject of Clauses 4 through 11 of the bill.
First of all, I would like to review briefly the historical background to these oil export charges. In doing so I hope to be able to point out how these oil export charges fit into the framework of longstanding Canadian oil export policy, how the federal government has responded to the needs and interests of the provincial governments, has responded to the regions of Canada as well as to the needs of the oil product industry, in terms of introducing, negotiating and administering those oil export charges. Oil export charges are big business. I understand that in the fiscal year 1981-82 the National
Energy Board collected charges amounting to $700 million- big business indeed.
Members of the House will note from Clause 7 of the bill before us that the National Energy Board, on behalf of the minister, actually administers and enforces the part of the Petroleum Administration Act that I am dealing with. I would like the House to note that the board has carried out this task since 1974 and has done so with great efficiency, using a minimum of human and financial resources in the process. The 1981 National Energy Board report will give some details concerning the board's involvement in the administration of this part of the act.
Members of the House will recall that the taxing of domestic source oil exports started back in October, 1973. Shortly before that, the Government of Canada had requested the Canadian oil industry not to increase further crude oil prices, which had been rising for about a year as prices in the United States and overseas increased. However, the opportunity-price in export markets continued to rise as a result of international events. The National Energy Board required and still requires that export prices should be just and reasonable in the Canadian public interest.
The board set an export price for October, 1973 which exceeded the domestic price. The government therefore acted to obtain for Canada, to obtain for Canadians, the difference between the domestic price and the available export price by means of a tax. The authority for this tax from October, 1973 to March, 1974 was the Oil Export Tax Act. Incidentally, this particular act was administered by the Department of National Revenue. The National Energy Board became responsible for administration of oil export charges as of April, 1974.
Understandably, the producing provinces were seriously concerned that the federal government should be appropriating revenue, part of which they thought should properly accrue to them, the producing provinces, in the form of royalty on higher export prices. This is something to which the opposition has frequently drawn attention in the past, arguing that the federal government was insensitive to provincial interests.
I want to take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to remind the House that all of the revenue collected by the federal government under the oil export tax in respect of exports from October, 1973 to January, 1974 was paid to the governments of the provinces from which the oil was deemed to have come. This meant that the provincial government benefited not just to the tune of a deemed royalty, perhaps one-fifth of the value of the oil export, but rather they enjoyed 100 per cent of the revenue from those export sales.
The circumstance for February and March of 1974 was different. As a result of the agreement reached at the first ministers' conference in January, 1974, the federal government had by early 1974 undertaken an obligation to shield the import-dependent eastern part of the country from dramatically rising international prices, a policy that has worked very
April 26, 1982

much to the benefit of the people in my riding of Burin-St George's and the people of Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada generally. The government provided this shield against dramatically rising international oil prices, by means of the oil import compensation program which continues in effect as a means to achieve a single oil price across Canada at levels much below those prevailing internationally.
Because of this large new financial obligation undertaken by the Government of Canada-undertaken, by the way, with the full agreement of all provinces-the producing provinces agreed that the federal government could keep half of the royalty from export tax revenue accruing from exports made in February and March, 1974. The other half, like the revenues from the period October, 1973 to January, 1974, was to be paid to the governments of the provinces from which the oil was deemed to have come. Again, these governments, it goes without saying, benefited to a much greater extent than would have been the case under then prevailing royalty regimes.
The authority to apply a charge on oil exports from April, 1974 until now stems from the Petroleum Administration Act, Part I. This is the portion of the legislation which Bill C-103, the bill we are dealing with here, seeks to amend in some important respects. All of these revenues from April, 1974 until October, 1980 accrued to the federal government.
I think it is worth while to remind ourselves again that it was by agreement with the producing provinces that all of the revenues between April, 1974 and October, 1980 would accrue to the Government of Canada. The agreement was secured at the March, 1974 first ministers' conference when it was also agreed to increase Canadian crude oil prices by what was then the very large amount of $2.70 a barrel effective April 1, 1974. I believe it is worth stressing that the federal government's access to those revenues was not achieved by a unilateral act of the Government of Canada but, rather, by agreement with the provincial governments concerned. That was the situation prevailing up until the announcement of the National Energy Program on October 28, 1980.
That briefly is the history of the oil export charge during part of which time all the revenues accrued to the federal government and during part of which time the revenues were split between the federal government and the governments of the producing provinces from which the oil was deemed to have come.
The National Energy Program documents noted that virtually all of the crude oil now exported from Canada is heavy crude oil. This oil is surplus to Canadian needs simply because Canada does not have the refinery capacity to use it. The National Energy Program includes measures to build an upgrader in Saskatchewan to turn this heavy crude oil into a product which can be processed in Canadian refineries. Incidentally, progress toward achievement of this objective of building a heavy crude oil upgrader in Saskatchewan has, according to the project's proponents, been somewhat hampered by the absence of definition of the fiscal regime which will apply to the enhanced oil recovery required to provide a
Energy Administration Act
stable, long-term feedstock supply for the heavy crude upgrader.
The National Energy Program went on to express the expectation that other upgraders would be built in either Saskatchewan or Alberta and that existing refineries would be modified so that they can use an increasing proportion of this heavy oil. Therefore, it was expected that there would be a progressive diversion of these export volumes into the domestic market. In the meantime, in the view of the government and as expressed in the National Energy Program, it seemed only fair to examine how the revenues from crude oil export charges should be shared among governments.
As I have noted, between April, 1974 and October, 1980 neither the Alberta government nor the government of Saskatchewan gained any benefit from the higher earnings which were available on crude oil exports as opposed to those on crude oil sold in the domestic Canadian market. The Government of Canada therefore indicated its intention to share with these two producing provinces 50 per cent of the export charge revenue on crude oil exports found by the National Energy Board to be surplus to Canada's needs and which are now subject to oil export charges. The program proposed that sharing would begin effective November 1, 1980.
Perhaps there are those in the House who would like to pursue that aspect of the National Energy Program in more detail. If so, I refer them to the program, and particularly to pages 36 and 37 of it which outline the proposal of the Government of Canada to share the oil export charge revenues with the two producing provinces of heavy crude, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
It is worth noting, especially for the benefit of detractors of this legislation or people who are detractors of the National Energy Program, that here is an example of an important initiative taken by the Government of Canada as part of its National Energy Program to share the revenues on a 50-50 basis with the producing provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The government has now presented the House with legislation intended to put this provision of the National Energy Program into effect. That, in essence, is what Bill C-103 is all about. It is to give effect to this important revenue-sharing provision. Clause 10 of the bill before us provides that the minister may make expenditures out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund for payment of such amounts as are authorized by the governor in council to be paid to a province or its agent in respect of exports of oil from that province during the year. I am sure the House welcomes the provision that the federal government is making, despite its own heavy fiscal burdens and responsibilities. It is a provision to divide crude oil export charge revenues in this way with the governments of the provinces from which the exported oil comes in the first instance.
Having spent just a little time on the history of this oil export charge and having spent just a little time outlining the objective of the legislation before us, I want to comment on the way in which the oil export charge is set. The charge is fixed

April 26. 1982
Energy Administration Act
by the governor in council on the recommendation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, taking into account, among other things, the advice of the National Energy Board.
Essentially export charges reflect the difference between the Canadian price for particular grades of crude oil and oil products and the export market price prevailing at the time. The charges which have eventuated from this procedure are set out in Schedule I to the bill for the period from May, 1979 onward. It was, of course, from that date, May, 1979, that the charge necessary in order to capture for Canada the difference between the available export price and the domestic price exceeded the maximum amount of the charge authorized by Parliament in the Petroleum Administration Act. The original maximum was $8 a barrel, or just over $50 a cubic metre. The government of the day, which was not this particular administration but the one which preceded it, found that the necessary level of these charges exceeded the amount authorized by Parliament. The exporting companies were notified by the government of the day, the administration led by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), that parliamentary authority would be sought at the earliest opportunity for such a higher level of charge, and meanwhile the companies were asked to remit-and they did, of course-at the higher level pending the setting in place of the appropriate legislation.
As I have just said, these charges from May, 1979 are set out in the schedule which is on page 39 of the bill before us. I want to point out that the administration of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition in 1979 followed exactly the same practice as the Liberal government before it in respect of the item before us now.
The level of the crude oil export charge has an obvious impact on the ability of producers to sell their oil in export markets. In setting the export charge the government has to achieve two basic objectives. First, it has to establish an export charge so that the export charge in total is just and reasonable in the Canadian public interest. That means putting it as high as is reasonably possible.
Second, it has to ensure that the export price is competitive and that oil surplus to Canadian requirements is fully taken up in the export market and is not shut in in order that the development of Canadian heavy crude oil reserves is not impeded. There is currently a problem of shut-in heavy oil production in western Canada and this is a matter of serious concern to the government.
As hon. members know, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) acted vigorously to deal with the problem of shut-in heavy oil production in western Canada. At the beginning of April he announced an action program which included measures intended to secure an export market for as much heavy crude oil as the National Energy Board found to be surplus to our own refinery requirements. The action program included a clear declaration that the Canadian export price would continue to be strongly competitive, that Canadian supply would be reliable, and that the National Energy Board
would be prepared to receive applications for longer term export licences.
In an effort to ensure full dialogue and information on this very important subject and this very important bill, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced an action program on April 1. I presume hon. members already have copies of this and, if not, they are readily available. The document is entitled "Securing Markets for Western Canadian Crude Oil-Program of Action." Among other things, the program includes the assurance that Canadian heavy crude oil exports to the United States will continue to be competitively priced by adjusting the export charge as required. It makes the provision that applications to the National Energy Board for the export of crude oil for terms of up to one year would be welcome. The policy remains to export heavy crude oil that is surplus to our domestic needs. In short, that particular program addresses in a very tangible way the problem of shut-in heavy oil production in western Canada.
I have gone into this matter of the purpose of the export charge, the way in which it is set and the objectives which the government follows in some detail because of the importance of the export charge in aggregate terms and because it has been the focus fo some attention relative to the problem of shut-in heavy western Canadian crude oil. I am satisfied that the government has shown the right degree of sensitivity to industry and producing province interests in dealing with this aspect of our national energy policy. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I believe the government has to show, and shows, a great deal of sensitivity in dealing with these difficult on going policy and operational problems.
Members will be aware that Part I of the Petroleum Administration Act provides for charges which are applicable also to refined oil products derived from Canadian crude oil. The purpose is to ensure that the people of Canada, rather than the exporting company, generally an oil refiner, benefit from the difference between Canadian and international oil prices when the product is refined from low-priced domestic crude oil and sold into a high-priced export market. This aspect of the oil export charge program has been successfully implemented for a number of years.
Members may be wondering how exports of oil products derived from imported crude oil are treated. So far, the oil export charge has been applicable only to domestic crude origin oil products. The government has, however, fully safeguarded the Canadian public interest by requiring companies which import foreign crude oil, and receive import compensation for it, to refund the full amount of the import compensation embodied in any products which are derived from such foreign crude oil and are subsequently exported. I can assure the House that the Canadian public and fiscal interest is fully safeguarded by this procedure.
Members will, however, have noted that Clause 5 of Bill C-103 makes provisions that a tariff of charges in respect of any or all of the various kinds or qualities of oil be set, regardless of the source of that oil, meaning whether that oil is of domestic or imported origin. This would give the government the
April 26, 1982

flexibility, should the need arise, to provide for an export charge for all oils crossing the border to export, rather than having two systems, one of export charging and one of import compensation refunding as at present. 1 for one welcome this provision as giving the government a sensible degree of flexibility.
It is, of course, understood that, if oil products are exported from foreign crude oil, then if an export charge is levied the exporter would not also have to refund the import compensation. One way in which this flexibility could be employed would be to enable a third party-an independent oil company, for example-to export foreign origin oil products to the United States without having to identify the original importer of the crude oil and pay back the compensation through that original recipient of compensation, as is presently the case.
The House has a complex piece of energy legislation before it. This is undeniable. However, I think the House should note that the Petroleum Administration Act has been in effect since 1974, with some relatively minor amendments made in 1978. The powers it provides have been used by the Progressive Conservative party when in office as well as by successive Liberal governments. The Petroleum Administration Act under governments of two different party stripes has served the taxpayers of this country very well. It has stood the test of time.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend would find it convenient to take issue with that particular statement. I would remind him that in doing so he takes issue with the actions of the administration of which he was a member. The Progressive Conservative administration used without any change at all the Petroleum Administration Act which had been implemented by the former Liberal administration of 1974.
You did not give us a chance to change it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: The hon. member is still fighting the election.
Who brings it up all the time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: The people of Canada spoke very clearly in February, 1980.
Tell them that today in Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
If anyone did not give the Tory administration a chance, I submit it was that administration itself. It had just about a year to do something. That is the plea; that is the mea culpa we hear now-that they never had time. They know full well-and they would be more appreciated by the Canadian people if they owned up to it-that they did not change this piece of legislation because it has served this country well since 1974 and will continue to serve it well with some refinements as proposed in Bill C-103. This act, Mr. Speaker, has stood well the test of time. My hon. friend may not like that, but it is true.
Energy Administration Act
The changes in Part I of the Bill before us, to which my comments have been directed, seem to me to be both sensible and very desirable. They legislate charges beyond the scope of the original bill which started with the Progressive Conservative government in May, 1979. They provide for appropriate use of metric units and add some flexibility in terms of adjustments to the charge even for part of a month. They enable the charge to apply to foreign crude products, and provide that a government can make payments out of oil export charge revenues to provinces or their agents. All of these changes are necessary and in the public interest.
So there it is, an eminently sensible bill. A bit complicated, perhaps, but out of necessity because of the nature of the subject it deals with. It is sensible legislation based on fairness and the principle of sharing, a principle which we on this side not only espouse but do something about in our legislation. The sharing in this case is between the Government of Canada on behalf of all the people and the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta on behalf of their people. This legislation preserves the essential spirit of the Petroleum Administration Act of 1974, which enjoyed the active support not only of the government which brought it in in 1974 and of the current government, but which also enjoyed the active support of the short-lived Tory administration in 1979.
There is nothing sinister, underhanded or conniving about this particular bill, Mr. Speaker. That must disappoint my hon. friend but it is true. It is just a straightforward bill which sets about bringing the legislation in line with reality. It sets about updating a mechanism which has served us well since 1974 and now, with some refinement, can continue to serve us well. What we have in Bill C-103 is of considerable benefit to the taxpayers of Canada, and those taxpayers of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Can there really be anyone in this House who opposes such sharing? Can there really be anyone here who would dare to oppose such fairness in revenue sharing?
The argument was that the government's omnibus bill, which was earlier before the House, had lumped together too many things. They said it included measures which members would want to support with those which they might want to oppose. This bill presents no such dilemma, Mr. Speaker. No one is caught here in the conundrum of saying; "Well, I want to vote for this part but I cannot vote for that part". Here, Mr. Speaker, the issue is very clear-cut and simple, and it is this: Do we as members of this House support sharing oil export revenues with the producing provinces? That is the essential issue. Members either support that or they do not. Members can come up with all kinds of reasons, excuses or canards as to why they would like to support it, but, however, they are going to be clearly on the record on this one.
The challenge is to put your money where your mouth is. Either you support the initiative taken by this government to

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
share on a 50-50 basis these revenues with the producing provinces, or you do not support it. Do members of this House believe the people of Canada should benefit financially from oil exports? If members believe that, it is clear where their vote will be when the question is called on this particular piece of legislation.
This is a good piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, because it seeks to embody a principle, as this government has so often done in legislation, which is the cornerstone of the Liberal party and of this particular government-sharing among Canadians the benefits we reap from the extraction of our resources. That, when all the i's have been dotted and the t's have been crossed, is the clear issue which remains. Let no one try to befuddle that. The issue is not whether we should have an export charge, which we have had since 1974; anyone who opposes that concept is about eight years too late. The issue is whether some members of this House can put aside their partisanship, their natural propensity to give it to the government every time they have a chance, their natural temptation to exercise the opposition mentality which says: if the government proposes it, I am "agin" it. It is time to put all that aside and answer two basic questions: do I as a member of this House believe that the people of Canada should benefit financially from oil exports? The answer to that is an unequivocal yes. I am sure I speak for every member of this House; the answer must be an unequivocal yes or that member has no business being here. The second question is: do I support the concept of sharing export oil revenues with the producing provinces? The answer to that question is also an unequivocal yes. I believe it ought to be and is an unequivocal yes for every member in this chamber. If it is not, then that hon. member has no business being here. The entire Canadian experience has no meaning if we do not believe in the concept of sharing, sharing the benefits which derive from the extraction of resources across this country.
For those reasons, and for so many other good reasons that I could state if time were available to me, I want to say that I am going to support this bill with a heart and a half and I would expect that every other member in the House will do likewise.

Mr. Speaker, in listening to the address of the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) I had difficulty deciding in which country he was living and which bill he is discussing. The issue, as I see it, is entirely different from the one he outlined to the House a few moments ago.
The issue in this bill is whether or not the people of Canada are going to pay more than 50 cents a gallon extra for their gasoline and whether the government will do this without reference to the Parliament of Canada. That is one of the reasons why the bells rang. These things should be decided by the Parliament of Canada and not by the cabinet of the country. The issue in the mind of the hon. member for Burin-St. George's is very confused. Either he has the wrong bill or the wrong country.
For a few moments I want to deal with some of the points that he made concerning the benefits that the people of Canada from coast to coast are receiving from the National Energy Program and the energy legislation. Instead of just talking theory, I will try for a few moments to describe to hon. members the situation out west where the oil is produced. Over the last two years there has been a tremendous change in the oil industry. It has gone from being a buoyant industry to an industry that is now sliding down, down and down. First is the matter of investment money. People are not prepared to invest their money in the oil industry given the uncertain terms resulting from the policies being followed by the administration in Ottawa. For example, all hon. members have to do is to look at the type of legislation that is being brought forward. One piece of legislation enabled Petro-Canada on behalf of the government on behalf of Petro-Canada to expropriate part of the oil findings of another company after it had spent money finding oil, and at the same time paying nothing at all to a company that had spent a couple of million dollars only to come up with a dry hole.
The oil industry was buoyant two years ago. It is now depressed. Things are as bad now as they were at any period in our history. Rig after rig, many employees and pieces of equipment have left the country. People have not left the country because they were rich or because they could not do well here. The multinationals can look after themselves. But the independent companies are the ones suffering. The independent operators have left the country because they could not make a profit. The oil industry is slowly dying. Money is drying up and there is no incentive to find oil or gas. The policies of the government have driven out the independents. The energy program and federal legislation are the main culprit in this gigantic exodus of industry, expertise, equipment and people from Canada to the United States. We had a tremendous network of expertise, equipment and men which had been built up by the small companies starting from scratch and developed into network of large companies. A tremendous group of people were developing the industry and making a profit. But when the profit disappeared, the small independents were unable to stay in business and had to leave.
The policies which the hon. member for Burin-St. George's mentioned and which he praised so highly, have driven these people out of the country. Our expertise has left. Our rigs have left. Do not kid yourself by saying that they were the rich or the stingy who wanted to hog more and more. All they wanted to do was what they did for several years, namely, make a living and contribute to the country. They are just as anxious to contribute to the country as is any other person in this land of ours. The suggestion that this is a wonderful program just does not bear examination when one takes time to look at the results of it. People should look at the results of a program and the legislation, not just the administration of it. The results show a sad picture indeed.
If hon. members visited almost any town in Alberta or Saskatchewan, they would be able to find out how the people feel. The industry is drying up. There is no incentive to drill. In
April 26, 1982

fact, there is no incentive at all. Elon. members can quote all the figures they like, but I tell them to look at the lists of unemployed. This energy program not only affects the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan but it affects all Canadians. Eastern Canadians and central Canadians went out west, got jobs and then found their jobs gone as a result of the National Energy Program. This has greatly increased the unemployment lists and the applications for unemployment insurance in the city of Calgary. The increase in applications for unemployment caused the government to send more and more administrative people from eastern Canada to Calgary. I can speak about the situation in Calgary, but I suppose the same is true for the city of Edmonton. There are masses of applications for unemployment insurance. If nothing else tells this government what is wrong, surely that tells the government things are not buoyant any more. People are not investing any more and they are leaving the country.
People who have never before been unemployed in their lives before who are now unemployed. The effects of this energy policy are being felt in small towns by restaurant owners and by hotel owners. Everyone is being affected. The National Energy Program and the energy legislation have created a depression. If that is the kind of result which the hon. member for Burin-St. George's was talking about, the result of a program which was supposed to benefit the people from coast to coast, he had better tell me who it is benefiting in Alberta, Saskatchewan, or the maritimes. It is benefiting very few people in central Canada.
The situation became so bad that the government of Alberta decided to do something about it because the agreement and a number of other things had resulted in havoc, depression, unemployment, a lack of investment, and people leaving the country. This is not theory, this is reality. People are still leaving the country. The government of Alberta decided that it would have to do something to keep the industry from deteriorating any further. During the last two years under the Liberal administration of the federal government the industry was sliding, so the Alberta government came up with a program. It said that it would contribute 8 per cent of the government's cash flow over the next five years and that it would cut down the profit of government to see if it could get the industry moving, get jobs created, get people working and increase the net worth of production. The government of Alberta also said that it would raise the basic price to cover exploration, investment and development costs and that it would increase that amount by reducing the amount of royalties. The amount was $1.7 billion over five years, or an average of $340 million per year, which the government of Alberta would put into the industry to help it keep its head above water. This is what the Alberta government did.
When we talk about sharing, we must remember that the Alberta government is giving up some of its revenues to keep the industry moving and to provide jobs so that wives and children will not have to depend upon welfare. It will provide
Energy Administration Act
$1.7 billion over a five-year period. It plans to do the same for the gas producing industry, which will cost $2 billion. It extended the holiday for royalty payments for new wells, costing $1.5 billion, and set up $250,000 in grants for service and maintenance work this summer. It is putting money into the pockets of people now, not months ahead or five years from now. The government of Alberta has taken a positive step. In the meantime, world prices of oil have declined and world demand for oil has reduced. These factors must be looked at as well.
The Alberta program will not solve the problem of the sharp cutback in Alberta production because of federal government subsidies which make it cheaper for eastern refineries to buy foreign crude. That is another matter about which people are not happy. I do not think people in Ontario either or in Quebec can understand why we are importing crude from Mexico while wells are closed up in Saskatchewan and Alberta. Men have been laid off, the industry is depressed, but we put money into the pockets of those who keep people in jobs in other countries.
It is difficult to understand the thinking of a government which does that type of thing. It talks about importing crude and keeping our own wells tied up and our industry depressed. It will not even allow the export of Alberta light crude which would put people to work. The $1.7 billion over a five-year period will help get industry moving again, as long as the federal government does not try to hog some of it. This point is very important in the minds of industrial people in Alberta today. While Premier Lougheed was doing something positive to revive the oil industry, to create jobs and to provide some profit, the federal government has decided to take it away.
What is the federal government doing? It is providing $4.9 billion in additional capital to Petro-Canada and another $5 billion in compensation payments related to world price. The Alberta government amends the damage of the National Energy Program and the agreement, but the Government of Canada continues to fill its coffers under the leadership of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). Had the government been sincere when the Alberta government made its offer, it would have said, "We will do the same thing. We will also give up some of our profits and some of our excess money so that it can be put into the industry to keep jobs". This is what the Government of Canada should have done. Now the people of western Canada are afraid that the federal government will hungrily grab from the industry part of what the Alberta government put out to help it survive and keep its head above water.
Certainly the Government of Canada is looking for trouble. The people of western Canada are reaching the breaking point. Their own government has gone the second mile in trying to keep the industry in business and to stop bankruptcies. Heaven knows, there have been enough bankruptcies already! The Alberta government is attempting to stop them, but if the federal government steps in and starts grabbing some of the money there will be trouble.

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
Ottawa's priorities seem to lie in other areas. A few days ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that the total additional capital provided by this bill, that is the Petro-Canada amendments, would be $4.9 billion. He went on to say that the new capital ceiling it authorized was $5.5 billion, but that because $500 million had been subscribed under the present act, and since a further $100 million had been provided with respect to the interest in Panarctic Oils, the total of new capital funds available was $4.9 billion.
Then on April 6 the same minister said that they wanted to strengthen and expand Petro-Canada and increase its activities. He should not have much trouble when he is using public moneys as he is. The value to Petro-Canada of the Petrofina levy is $800 million a year out of the pockets of people, not out of the pockets of any government. It is coming out of the pockets of people who are depressed, people who are unemployed, people who are wondering from where they will get enough to feed their children. When the government grabs $800 million per year, it does not take long before it turns to billions. It will be taken from the car drivers of the country, not to produce or to create jobs, but to pay for Petrofina which was bought at a ridiculously high price. The shifting of ownership and control of the industry to Ottawa is only part of the game. It appears to the people of Canada who look at this that there is a shifting. Conventional people in Alberta could not find work and had to leave the country. Now it is being shifted to Petro-Canada. I am not opposed to Petro-Canada, but I am opposed to the centralization of power in the hands of this government. The primary objective of the national energy policy has always been to transfer the benefits from Alberta oil and gas to the politically powerful regions which maintain the central government in power. It does nothing for producers or the producing regions.
The transfer of this $5 billion in benefits from Alberta to a single central province was made specific in a speech which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources delivered to the Langelier Liberal Riding Association in Quebec City on June 1 of last year. The minister said something which the people of Canada and the people of Quebec should know about. When discussing the oil import compensation program, he said:
Under this program we have paid oil importers in the East-most of whom, as you know, are centred in Montreal-a subsidy which they will continue to receive and which is equal to the difference between the cost of a barrel of imported oil and the cost of the same barrel of oil when it is produced in Canada.
In other words, he is taking money from the rest of Canada and paying it to the importers in the city of Montreal. It is true that by this simple mechanism he has contributed generously to locking in 400,000 barrels a day of Alberta crude oil and robbing the people, government and corporations of the province of the jobs, revenues and opportunities that would result from the production of this crude oil. But the dollar losses in Alberta have popped up as dollar benefits elsewhere, such as to the people around Montreal. I wonder how that sounds to the people of Ontario, Manitoba, the Maritimes and
the rest of Quebecers. I do not think it will suit them very well. These are the minister's own words, when he talks about taking this money and continuing to put it into this particular area. He said further to the same group:
We have made a considerable financial investment in this program-
They certainly have.
-one which, over the course of the years, has amounted to several billion dollars and which represents a direct subsidy to the consumers of Eastern Canada, the majority of whom are Quebecers. It is not difficult to imagine the additional burden which would have to be borne by the budget of every citizen and every family in Quebec, were it not for this subsidy.
Those were the words of the minister of energy who is supposed to be representing Canada. He is taking money from one part of Canada and concentrating it in another specific part of Canada. It is true that the minister is Robin Hood; he is robbing the people of one part of Canada and giving it to- or what he calls sharing it with-people in another part of a province. The minister went on to say:
Thus, between 1973 and 1980, Quebecers have received five billion dollars in payments under this program, or $835 per capita.
Those were the words of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. This means that the two million people of Alberta donate to the six million in Quebec what amounts to some $3,000 to an average family there.
We in our province do not object to sharing. We have shared from the beginning. What other Canadian province has sold its non-renewable energy products, its oil, for less than it could get in other markets? Albertans have lost $18 billion in order to provide a better price for Canadians. They have shared as much, or more, than anyone else in Canada. When Albertans hear the minister making these comments and see those programs being implemented, it is no surprise that there is bitterness in our country. It is no wonder that Western Canada Concept is making progress. This government has the audacity to say that western members of Parliament are creating separatism. It is policies such as these which are creating separatism. Anyone who will be affected by these policies will not like them. While Quebecers will certainly accept the money if the government pours it into their province, they do not appreciate a policy such as this any more than anyone else. Quebecers want to contribute the same as the rest of Canada.
The Alberta government has released $5 billion of urgently needed stimulus for the benefit of all Canadians. The Government of Canada is doing its utmost to commit twice that amount of money for its own political purposes. What a shame!

Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, make a few preliminary remarks concerning the parliamentary events that made it possible for the House to examine Bill C-103 at 6.35 p.m. today, although normally, the House would have adjourned at 6 p.m., to resume sitting at 8 p.m. This goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that Parliament works when parliamentarians want it to work.
April 26, 1982

I had an opportunity to speak in the debate on a motion by the Right Elon. Leader of the Opposition, the day after the parliamentary impasse ended. We were discussing plans for parliamentary reform in terms that showed that hon. members who spoke in the debate felt a real urgency that the work of the Elouse should be as relevant as possible.
Today, I would like to take this opportunity to express once more the hope that very soon, Parliament, either through referral to the Committee on Procedure and Organization or in some other way, will be able to formulate concrete proposals to ensure that, in the future, the House of Commons will not be reduced to the pitiful exercise that paralysed it for more than two weeks.
At the time, I also said that some good would come out of all this, and today, an agreement made by the three House Leaders has made it possible to reach a consensus on a package of extremely complex legislation-which sparked the deadlock in the first place-and split the original bill into eight separate bills, so that each party and each member of the House could make a real contribution to the legislative process, which is the responsibility of this House, and in turn, allow the government which, we presume, is here to govern, to apply time allocation, a system not frequently used in this House but common practice in other countries and in other jurisdictions, especially at Westminster, the model for our Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be speaking in the debate today, because I find these parliamentary events extremely important, and because I hope that in the future, without resorting to dilatory tactics like those used originally to split the bill, we will be able to work together in the same spirit and reconcile parliamentary responsibilities with the role of government, which is to govern. I now conclude these marginal notes on the events that have taken place in Parliament, which are, I feel, important because since this agreement we have been working in an orderly fashion, bills have been subjected to thorough debate, they have been voted on sincerely and conscientiously by members on both sides of this House, and finally, they have been the subject of a debate the public had a right to expect in the circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, it is often said that money is the life-blood of wars. 1 think it is probably a truism to say that energy is the motor of society as we know it today. Whether it is used to run our factories or our cars, during this century, cheap energy has enabled so-called industrial societies to prosper, to develop and to enable its citizens to live richer if not better lives, and has made it possible to achieve during this century a rate of growth hitherto unknown in the history of man.
Cheap energy-there you have a paradox, Mr. Speaker. The debate on Bill C-103 is an opportunity to point out how extraordinary it is that, today, people are complaining because
Energy Administration Act
the price of energy or perhaps I should say energies, is at the centre of public attention, while for 50 years we ignored the entire question and were using resources which are, by definition, mankind's capital reserves, namely, our non-renewable resources. In 1973, the first energy crisis occurred when the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries decided-1 may add that it probably had every reason to do so-to draw the best possible benefits from the income constituted by the price paid for oil, especially since most of these countries had no other resources. Oil is taken from the desert or the ocean floor and may come from developing countries that must use this resource windfall to promote the development of their own society. Is it therefore so surprising that, after this psychological and economic shock, Canada, so richly endowed but also dependent on foreign sources of oil and gas, should want to develop its own national energy policy? The cynics among us would claim that an energy policy is long overdue. But, and I say it once again, before 1973 energy was cheap and in abundant supply, and we took advantage of it, in an almost orgiastic consumption of oil and gas, without worrying about who was going to pay the bill and where the energy was coming from.
At the end of the sixties, I remember reading in the papers about the most far-fetched projections that Canada would be self-sufficient in oil and gas for at least 100 or even 150 years. The fact that known reserves were diminishing proved nothing, since in any case, there was an arbitrariness about the whole issue, and the oil companies with their vast monopolies could, in fact, say what they chose to whom they chose. What a shock, after 1973, when we realized that Canada did, in fact, have the capability of being self-sufficient in energy but that we would have to pay a high price to attain that self-sufficiency. Why have a national energy policy? Because I think that Canadians realized at a certain point in their history that it was important and even imperative for us as a society to be able to exercise some control over our own destiny. That is more or less the philosophy underlying the national energy policy, and I support it. I do not think any members in this House could be opposed to this concept.
We want to achieve energy self-sufficiency in Canada and we have the means to do so, even where oil is concerned, but we still have to implement a consistent policy to deal with all the problems which this goal raises with respect to supply, compensation, prices, taxes, charges, allowances, research and development, as well as frontier production. So, we have a national energy policy, and it was announced by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde); but now, several months later, a year and a half to be exact, we are still discussing in this House how to implement this policy. Implementing a national energy policy is not an easy exercise because you essentially have to rely on unpredictable factors over which you have no control. While it is true that 18 months ago we could forecast, because of events which have

And Petro-Canada is nothing else but a lever to allow Canadians to play an active role in applying the principles contained in the National Energy Program. Some might retort that Petro-Canada will use public funds to compete with companies that must go to the financial markets in order to explore, develop, produce the oil and gas needed. That is true. But is there anything wrong, Mr. Speaker, with the reason why we proposed the establishment of Petro-Canada, that Canadians should be directly involved in oil exploration and production? A joint rather than an exclusive interest. Personally, I see nothing wrong, Mr. Speaker, with the fact that through a tax levied on a litre of gas Canadians are involved in the purchase of Petrofina and the establishment of an entity capable of participating with other members of the industry in the implementation of our energy objectives. Let me get to the question of the whole idea of a Canadian oil price. That idea was first presented by the Hon. Bob Stanfield when the first increase in oil prices took place. He suggested that somewhere along the line we ought to try to minimize the shock of going to world prices. For a period of time bit by bit we worked our Canadian price up very close to the world price. That was the situation until 1978 or 1979. The OPEC people then again decided to go on a rampage, and world prices advanced dramatically. This government went to the country with the concept of a Canadian price. At that point the price of oil in Canada was controlled under the Petroleum Administration Act and was considerably less than the price of oil in other parts of the world. This government said it would continue to keep the price of oil and oil products significantly lower than the price in other parts of the world. As long as that was the case we in Canada had an advantage because we had petroleum and petroleum products available for our industry, to heat our homes and to drive our transportation vehicles at a price lower than that which prevailed in other parts of the world. In a sense we were using our resources sensibly to give our country a competitive advantage.
The national energy policy and the philosophy expressed in this bill ceased to do that. Instead of providing an advantage to Canadians it became the policy to tax Canadian resources and to see if the Ottawa government could get as much money in tax dollars as conceivably possible from the oil industry on oil from the ground or on oil which passed through the refining and processing systems. The provincial governments saw what was happening, and certainly the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and the eastern provinces decided they might as well join in the game because no longer was it the policy of the Government of Canada to produce petroleum products in Canada at a price which would give Canadian industry and Canadian transportation a price advantage over the rest of the world. The policy was clearly a policy to tax, tax and tax. Last year the revenues of the Government of Canada increased 22 per cent in one year. They have increased 40 per cent over two

years, and that revenue increase is largely the result of the monster taxes imposed on the oil industry by this bill and related statutes.
This bill deals with two principal forms of taxation and a third form of taxation in terms of transportation fuel. First, it deals with what is called the petroleum compensation fund, which is a tax on petroleum products in Canada. Presumably it is to tax oil in order to collect enough to pay for the cost of bringing down the price of imported oil and to bring about some sort of average Canadian price.
The second tax in the bill deals with some concept which has absolutely nothing to do with energy security but everything to do with socialism, nationalization and seizure of private property. It is a tax on every gallon or barrel-or cubic metre now-of fuel to enable the purchase of new oil companies or to make new oil investments by the Government of Canada. These investments are not to be made by individual Canadians but by the Government of Canada through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) so that the minister and his advisers, who certainly have no love for private enterprise or the free entreprise system, can become the largest owners and controllers of the oil industry.
If the policy were to produce oil and oil products as cheaply as possible for Canadians-bearing in mind the problem of security-and to average the price down so that Canadians would have a competitive advantage in the world and so that Canadian industry and business and the jobs which could be created would have a competitive advantage, then we could support it, but that is not the policy. This is a policy of taxation to bring in more and more revenue, and it is being sold as a policy of energy security. It is being sold as a policy of Canadi-anization. It is really a policy of control, a taxation policy, and it ought to be viewed by my friends on the government side as exactly that.
If the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had come into the House and said,"We feel that gasoline is the same as liquor and we are going to tax it in the same way; we feel that gasoline and home heating oil are the same as wine and we are going to tax them in the same way-get all we can from them and then reduce other taxes", he might not have found an argument. But this has been presented to us as energy security which is good for the country and will make us self-sufficient. We all know that the policy has not made us self-sufficient, has not encouraged drilling, has not encouraged production, has not encouraged jobs-it is a policy designed solely to get as much out of the industry as possible and to put it in the hands of the spenders in government and thus give government control over what goes on.

Bill C-93 deals with the PGRT and excise taxes. This bill has the same principle, that is, that the tax limits are upper limits and taxes can be raised to those limits or reduced. They can be fiddled around in any way that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) or the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) suggests to the governor in council. For the first time in our history, in Bill C-93 and in Bill C-103, there comes a time when the Minister of Finance-or in this case the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources-has the right to raise or lower taxes. Through this bill the minister reserves to himself, not to parliament but to himself, the right to levy taxes.

The whole purpose of parliament, dating back to 1215, is to determine how and by whom taxes may be levied.
