It has only upper limits and the great wonderful world in which the government gets more, more and more. Perhaps the oil companies get a little more? Do they? The price is going down for sure, but the taxes do not go down; therefore, the netback to the industry must go down, and that is where we stand.
With respect to the national energy policy and I am reading from a news release appearing on the minister's own stationery, dated September 1, 1981, which stated that for Canadian consumers the bottom line is that they have fair oil and gas prices. Already Canadian consumers are getting fair prices? They are getting "fairly hooked" more than anybody else, certainly more than anybody else in North America. The
Energy Administration Act
industry does not get the money to get on with the job. I thought we would go on to that right now, Mr. Speaker, because you and I know that as a result of this policy, drilling in Canada in 1981 over 1980 is down 25 per cent. Compare that with the 25 per cent increase in the United States. Well completions in 1981 amounted to 7,183 compared with 9,481 in 1980. That is another 25 per cent drop. Exploratory drilling is down 19 per cent. Developing drilling is down 28 per cent. In terms of metres drilled, the decline was from 10.27 million metres in 1980 to 7.64 million metres in 1981. That is another 25 per cent drop.
Two hundred and twenty six drilling rigs left Canada. This was all for the "security of supply," to make sure that we have more expensive oil. It made sure that the industry was less efficient, and the advantage that Canadians had up until 1979 and into the early part of 1980 has dissipated and gone. The advantage which Canadians had over the Europeans has gone. The advantage which Canadians had over Americans in terms of energy, energy prices and energy availability has gone. What do we have instead? We have a tax regime that increased taxes last year by 22 per cent. This regime will increase taxes 40 per cent over the two-year period. Do we see any lessening of other taxes? Not on your life. Income taxes are increased by the November budget for most people earning under $30,000 ayear. Fifty four per cent of people earning under $50,000 a year will pay more taxes. What about corporations? Corporate taxes are up dramatically. I say to you, Sir, that this is a bad bill and it must be defeated.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to add in this debate. I was quite taken by my colleague's comments on the acquisition of Petrofina. He expressed views that I find are being expressed across the country.
This bill, as mentioned by others, will establish a new ceiling for the petroleum compensation charge; a new oil export ceiling of $350 per cubic metre; the Canadian ownership special charge; and the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge.
The main concern I have is the amount of taxation being added on to oil and petroleum products generally. I recall, and I am sure you remember the time a few years ago, when the then minister of energy, the Hon. Alastair Gillespie, stood in the House and announced that as part of the conservation program of the government $100 would be added to the cost of air conditioning installed in an automobile. Most Canadians have forgotten about that, I am sure. As a matter of fact, in compiling an automobile price today, I do not believe the dealer even mentions this item. That $100 is added automatically. Any car a person buys with air conditioning in it costs an extra $100 in tax, and that tax goes directly to the government. That $100 was supposedly added for conservation purposes.

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
I want to go through the various charges that have been added on to oil, but at this point I want to tell hon. members what happens after a tax is added and is forgotten about.
Many people, particularly in the automobile industry, engineers and those who know about these things, laughed that the $100 charge would be a conservation measure. They pointed out, quite rightly, that if you drove your automobile with the windows open it would cost more in energy than air conditioning would. Also, if you drove a car with soft tires, it would cost more in energy than a car installed with air conditioning would. But there is a final irony to that particular tax. Some Canadians were so angry at the thought of paying this extra $100 that those who lived near the border went across to the United States into Buffalo, Detroit and other areas where service stations would install air conditioning. They bought it there and they did not have to pay the $100. Then another thing happened-the RCMP became involved. The RCMP made a deal with the guys across the border who were installing air conditioning. They paid them $20 for every Canadian license number which they could give them. Consequently, the fellow heard a knock on his door, and there would be an RCMP officer with a writ of assistance. His automobile was seized, he had to pay a fine plus the cost of the air conditioning, and he suffered much anguish. This went on for quite some time after the tax was put in place.
I should like to look at the various taxes on petroleum products. There is an export charge, a special levy, a Syncrude levy, a petroleum compensation charge, a Canadian ownership charge, a fuel compensation recovery charge, an import charge and a transportation charge. On top of all these are the federal excise tax and the provincial sales tax, except in the province of Alberta. If that is not overloading a product with taxation, I do not know what is. As far as I am concerned, it is part of the cause of the decline in our industry in the past 18 to 24 months.
There were people in the industry who thought that energy prices had to rise. They expected it. They recognized the world price and so on, but they had the feeling that regardless of this they still had it made because we had a great resource and somehow the government would arrange it so that we would always have a competitive advantage in the international field. The reality today, or part of the malaise in the economy today, is that they now realize that they are paying more. They look at the resource we have and see that heavy oil is on the shelf and, that the tar sands development has been put back. They hear the mythical talk about self-sufficiency by 1990. Along with them I do not believe we will achieve self-sufficiency by 1990. Part of the problem is the taxes and what is done with the money.
I want to talk about what happens to tax money, which is an important point. I recall three or four years ago a program called "Enersave" which was put in place by the Department
of Energy, Mines and Resources. I welcomed three young people into my constituency who were heading up the Enersave program. They told the people of my constituency that they worked for the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, but in reality they did not. They had obtained a grant of $90,000 to go out into the community to advise people on how to conserve energy. This is what it was all about. They were equipped to go into the schools to advise students on how to save energy. They could talk with representatives of school boards and municipal officials on how to save energy. They could talk to architects, engineers and owners of construction companies on the same subject. This is what they were telling me. I inquired as to their qualifications because I felt that if they were advising people on how to do things, they should have some basic knowledge.
This is what I discovered. The young lady heading the project was a professional program conductor. She had operated several LIPs, youth programs and so on. She had operated so many that I assumed she was looked upon by various government departments as a professional program director. She had as her assistants a third year history student from university and a fourth year high school student. I began to talk with them about how they felt when they talked with the man, for example, who designed the building in which their offices were located. I asked them whether they felt qualified to advise this man, who was an architect, on energy conservation matters. They said that they would take a crack at it. I asked them whether they felt confident talking with city engineers and advising them on saving energy for the city and so on. Then we got down to the final point-"What do you really know about the subject?" They held up a handful of pamphlets written by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. They had read the pamphlets, and that is all they knew about energy.
Also 1 talked to them about different kinds of oil such as heavy oil, light distilate, sweet oil, sour oil and gas. They did not have a clue. I am not being critical of those students. They were nice, keen, energetic, honest young people who really thought they were out doing something, but as far as I was concerned they wasted $90,000 of taxpayers' money in my constituency. In fact, after returning from a series of meetings at three o'clock in the morning on one occasion, at two o'clock in the morning on another occasion, and at four o'clock on another morning, I telephoned them because I saw that the lights in their office were on. I called them up and said, "If you are talking about conservation, at least turn off the lights in your own office".
The people who pay the taxes collected by the government and dispensed by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources are the ones who are asking questions which I am at a loss to answer. I should like to refer to a typical letter from a constituent who wrote in reply to an article which he read in
April 26, 1982

the April 15 edition of The Spectator in Hamilton. It was a story about Michael Phelps, executive assistant to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). The story was that Mr. Phelps had just made approximately $64,000 from the sale of a home he bought less than two years before with the help of an interest-free loan from the Petro-Canada Crown corporation; it gave all the financial details. A spin-off of that was the letter I received from Mr. R. I. Gowland of Burlington who wrote:
Dear Mr. Kempling:
I am inquiring as to my chances of obtaining a $35,000 interestfree loan from Petro-Canada (a Crown corporation). I would be willing to make payments of $31.25 a month for the first year and payments of $62.75 a month for the remainder of the loan.
Those were the terms which Mr. Phelps received in his agreement. The letter continued:
The figures I am quoting are from an article in The Hamilton Spectator April 15, 1982, that Mr. Michael Phelps (executive assistant to Energy Minister Marc Lalonde) received this type of loan in September 1980 and December 1980 from Petro-Canada.
As the mortgage on my home comes due the end of July 1982, the interest rates will increase from the present 10 per cent to 19.25 per cent, on a three year mortgage.
This will almost double my mortgage payments from $400 a month to $800 a month. My remaining mortgage at the present time is about $36,000, this loan would enable me to pay off my mortgage instead of losing my home. I do not want to make a profit from this transaction as Mr. Phelps did, I just don't want to lose my home.
Eagerly awaiting your reply.
Yours truly,
Ronald I. Gowland.
I read that story and wondered how I could answer this gentleman, because as far as I was concerned it was poor business to proceed in the manner of the minister and of Petro-Canada. If this is what is happening to the energy tax dollars which are being contributed by the people of Canada, I think it is wrong and we have a duty to point this out and rectify it wherever possible.
Aside from the Enersave program which I mentioned, where these three young people received a $90,000 grant, there is another Enersave operation in my constituency. Although I had difficulty finding out the background of this operation, I discovered there was a group of people who, supposedly, were representing Energy, Mines and Resources and who advised home owners on how to insulate their homes. They were funded through taxation derived from petroleum. I talked to these people in my constituency, as I usually do, and questioned them as to their competence, background and expertise in this field. I asked the person in charge what knowledge he had about energy and insulation. He did not know anything. He said, "I have a construction man on my staff who is my expert. I am an administrative expert." I then met the accountant and asked him the same question. He said that he
Energy Administration Act
was only in to set up the accounts and knew nothing about energy and insulation. I then met the construction expert. I have a great reverence for age and I respect elderly people but this gentleman could barely walk. He had a cane and had lost an eye. I honestly do not believe that he could climb a ladder to inspect an attic in order to determine what kind of insulation was needed. That was the staff of this organization.
I was quite intrigued by this operation since I come from the private sector where you must be very conscious of any conflict of interest which may arise as a result of which you may be charged with favouritism or fraud. I asked the leader of this operation how he conducted his business. He indicated that they put advertisements in the paper to which senior citizens and others would respond. He said, "These people want to have their homes insulated, and we advise them." I asked him how he gives this advice if he does not know anything about it. He indicated that he takes their names and addresses and sends the construction expert to inspect their homes. I told this person that his expert can hardly get in and out of a car, let alone climb a ladder to look in the attic. He said that they advised these people and told them what type of insulation they should buy. He said, for instance, "We tell them to buy fiberglass insulation." 1 asked him in what manner he gave this advice, and he said that he tells them which company to buy it from.
I said, "Let me give you some advice before you go any further. Do not tell people where to buy their insulation. If you want to give them an alphabetical list of insulation suppliers, that is fine." I indicated that these people should make their own choice so that he will not put himself in the position of indicating the company from which to buy insulation. Otherwise, he will discover many other companies accusing him of taking kickbacks and showing favouritism.
He accepted my advice but not before all the insulation contractors in the Burlington area had surrounded his business one day with all their vans and trucks to force a confrontation. That office closed down shortly after that incident. I understand that that operation had a budget of more than $150,000.
These two examples which I have cited represent $240,000 for projects which really have accomplished nothing. Therefore, when I see another bill which proposes to legitimize an ongoing tax or introduce more taxes, I sense that there is something wrong, or at least that there is a potential for questionable activities taking place. That is my concern.
When I review the CHIP program, which is still in existence in some manner, I believe we can honestly say that it was probably the most fraudulent program ever introduced by the government. Although this is unconfirmed, I am told there are approximately 8,000 pending charges under that CHIP program. These charges arise from a variety of circumstances. For example, there are contractors who did not perform the

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
job but charged for it. There are people who said they insulated their homes but did not actually do so. There are other examples as well.
When this CHIP program was at its peak, I recall distraught insulation contractors asking me for help because they were unable to collect thousands of dollars in accounts receivable. This was due to the fact that people who had their homes insulated would then apply to CMHC to receive money from Ottawa in order to pay the contractor. What happened was that they either did not receive the money or did not pay the contractors. Some home owners would tell the contractors that they had not yet received their money from the government, thus leaving the contractor with nothing. There are also incidents of counterfeit forms being printed. A used car dealer in Toronto would sell CHIP application forms for $5. A contractor would buy a $5 application form from this particular used car dealer, fill it out with his customer and process it in anticipation of receiving his money.
Another printing operation in Montreal sold bogus application forms, but only by the thousand. These forms cost $1 each. Those are only some examples from one of the most fraudulent programs ever introduced by the government.
There is not much left to be said about the UFFI situation. The way in which this program has been handled is an absolute disgrace. The minister has promised to rectify the problem, but it has merely been tossed over to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). He is releasing statements, one of which was a report released last Friday. But people who have their homes insulated with UFFI still do not know what will happen to them.
Like many of my colleagues and many Canadians, I have become most upset about the way in which the affairs of the nation are being conducted. This is particularly true with respect to energy. When the first OPEC increases came upon us, I do not believe that there was any concerned Canadian who would not have agreed that drastic steps had to be taken. I am sure they would have agreed that our objective should have been to become self-sufficient as soon as possible. If the government had come forward at that time and indicated that it would work closely with those oil producing provinces to help them develop the tar sands and their heavy oil and to attempt to make Canada self-sufficient not just by 1990 but as soon as possible, it would have had support. If this were to happen we would not be held at ransom by an offshore country. We should never allow that to happen again. Yet energy self-sufficiency, in spite of these added taxes, is still a myth to many of us. These policies will just continue and I doubt if you will ever see energy self-sufficiency. I doubt if we will see selfsufficiency by the turn of the century. We can look at what is going on in the Beaufort Sea and in Hibernia, off the Atlantic coast. I have no sense of conviction, from what I have read and from what I have been told by people who are knowledgeable in the industry, that we will have anywhere near sufficient
energy from that part of Canada by the turn of the century. Perhaps we will be lucky and technology will be developed to give us that oil off Hibernia.
We have become a little hardened to this whole matter. We have seen bills come forward, such as the omnibus bill, and we saw the massive power it would give to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to do all manner of things, such as power to raise taxes without consultation with Parliament and power to put new Crown corporations in place without consultation with the provinces, while most of the ones already in place are not operating on a profitable or even break-even basis today. Of course, we rebelled, and there was the incident which has become known as "the bells". While we have been criticized for that incident by hon. members opposite, I think hon. members on this side of the House feel that what we did was for the people of Canada.
We have the serious problem of unemployment in this country. What is happening to the oil industry is happening to almost all industries in Canada. Most of the people in the oil industry thought they had a sort of hidden economic advantage with the oil reserves and resources, and that a government with some common sense would help the provinces develop the resources, bringing them to Canadian industry to help get us out of our terrible balance of payments situation, reducing our unemployment and inflation, and curing all the ills which still seem to be upon us right now. However, the reality is that massive taxes are being taken from industry and from the people in general.
This is a vast country. We are a mobile people. When the source of the mobility is taken away; that is, the energy, and it is heavily taxed, then the people are isolated. They simply cannot travel that extra 40 or 50 miles to search out jobs, as they did a few years ago. It is not that long ago that people would travel a couple of hundred miles every day to and from their work. It might be easy to say that they should have moved nearer to their place of work, but they stayed where they were, for various reasons. However, today people say that they cannot afford $2 a gallon for gasoline to drive back and forth from Toronto to Hamilton or Kitchener to Toronto or from Niagara Falls to Toronto. Consequently, they just go on unemployment and look for employment within the area close to home. If they cannot find it, then they become part of the 1,200,000 unemployed in this country. I think that is a tragedy, as is the failure of the government to realize that this is weighing very heavily on all the people at this time.
With the amount of money which has gone into energy, it is almost impossible today to Find venture capital of any kind. There is a very negative attitude in the country, because we do not feel that the government has put programs forward which will ensure self-sufficiency in the foreseeable future. Therefore, people who generally have money available for venture
April 26, 1982

companies are simply not investing it, at least not in Canada. They are finding places to invest it outside Canada.
I will conclude my remarks here by saying I am sorry I cannot support this bill. I wish I could. I wish I could say this is a great bill and that it would help us become self-sufficient by 1987, 1986 or 1988. However, on the basis of this bill and the ones which have gone before it, I really cannot see that we will ever be self-sufficient until we have a complete change of thinking on the part of the people in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and in the government itself.
Mir. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources): Mr. Speaker, like hon. members who have previously spoken, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate. I believe it is critical that we act swiftly on the important measures contained in the bill and get on with the task of providing energy security, opportunity and fairness for all Canadians, which, in essence, are the major goals of the National Energy Program. This particular piece of legislation really touches on a number of items, five in particular, and I would very briefly like to describe each one.
First, the bill will establish a new ceiling of $75 per cubic metre for the petroleum compensation charge for the refiners and importers, and will broaden the scope for payment compensation to include new domestic oil.
Second, the bill will establish a new export charge ceiling of $350 per cubic metre and will provide us with authority to share one half of the revenue from this charge with the producing provinces. I am certain hon. members will appreciate that particular aspect of the amendment, in that 50 per cent of the revenue of the oil export charge would indeed go to the producing provinces. I do not believe hon. members, whether the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) or an hon. member from the province of Saskatchewan, would want to see those provinces denied 50 per cent of the revenues generated from that particular amendment.
They should get 100 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Third, it will establish the Canadian ownership special charge and the Canadian ownership account, and will ensure that the charge cannot be raised above its current level without additional legislation.
This bill will also establish the transportation fuel compensation recovery charge on marine and aviation fuel used by carriers in international transportation, with a ceiling of approximately $350 per cubic metre.
Finally, this piece of legislation will give authority for terminating the special compensation charge which was established at the time of the breakdown in negotiations with the government of Alberta.
We have heard a great deal from hon. members opposite, particularly those of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada who have spoken about the pricing of fuel oils here in
Energy Administration Act
Canada. However, our pricing system has three essential advantages over the regime proposed by the previous Conservative government in 1980.
First, it ensures that the prices will gradually and predictably rise so that consumers in the Canadian economy in general will have time to adjust. Second, it will ensure oil pricing fairness on a national level by providing a blended price to all regions of the country. Third, it will result in a consumer price which has, and will continue to be lower than that paid by people of most other countries. Those are the three succinct advantages of our pricing system over those offered by the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.
The National Energy Program was drafted with certain inescapable facts in mind. Canada is a country rich in energy, yet we currently import approximately 20 per cent of our oil needs. Conventional oil reserves in western Canada, the mainstay of this country for years, have shown a steady and marked decline in recent years. However, important new reserves of oil and gas are being found. For example, reserves of natural gas have grown from 1.7 billion cubic metres in 1970 to 2.6 trillion cubic metres in 1980. In addition to the oil sands of Alberta, with an estimated 48 billion cubic metres which may be technically recoverable, exploration and development in the frontier regions have turned up promising reserves of oil and natural gas.
Since the National Energy Program was introduced in this House on October 28, 1980, much has been accomplished by this government on energy policy. We even built an important part of the foundation for a more secure energy future based upon a rich endowment in natural resources, independent of the erratic prices and supplies on the international oil market. The energy legislation completes the building of that strong foundation and provides Canadians with the means to take control of their energy destiny.
Canadians from all walks of life can feel a growing sense of optimism and a sense of certainty about their energy in gas-producing provinces. The federal government now has energy agreements that provide fair prices for consumers and businesses and attractive incentives for Canada's petroleum companies to find more oil for Canada.
Those federal-provincial agreements were followed last December with the approval by this Parliament of the Canada Oil and Gas Act, a major and long overdue legislative initiative to manage development of the Canada lands in the frontier and offshore areas. Not only does the Canada Oil and Gas Act provide the federal government with a greater degree of control over the timing, direction and greater development in the northern and offshore lands, it also ensures that the people of Canada are given their rightful and equitable share in the building of their frontier energy industry.

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
1 intend to deal at some length with the petroleum administration act and, in particular, the petroleum compensation charge. First, let me deal with some of the wild accusations made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre. That hon. member has for several weeks now hurled remarks about energy-related matters at whoever would listen, beginning particularly with the Tory strike of Parliament. While he was receiving his salary from the Canadian taxpayer, he was throwing innuendoes all over the place. The hon. member for Calgary Centre has, without question, on many occasions misunderstood the various aspects of energy legislation, or inadvertently confused many aspects of the National Energy Program with every problem Canadians and other countries must face. Unfortunately the hon. member for Calgary Centre has not taken the time to thoroughly study the energy policy or the legislation of this government. On more than one occasion he has made public letters that he has written to various officials concerning government energy laws. For example, Bill C-48, the Canada Oil and Gas Act; the hon. member for Calgary Centre completely misunderstood the purpose of the legislation regarding renegotiation of the exploration rights on Canada lands.
Unfortunately the hon. member continues in the same old ways by throwing all kinds of rhetoric about the energy legislation before the House, Bill C-103. His speeches in the House lacked any kind of positive approach to the development of Canada's energy resources. The only contribution to serve our energy needs has been with natural wind power. It appears that the energy critic for the Conservative party and his colleagues have nothing to contribute to this very necessary debate, other than to throw wild accusations at the minister and attempt to fool the Canadian people, as they tried under the Crosbie budget, and we know what happened there-they failed.
This government has a plan of action for energy security in this country. It is outlined in the National Energy Program, and the various pieces of energy legislation now before the House will put our plan into action. This is one more sign of our commitment to our 1980 election promises, unlike the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary Centre who said in this House "the Liberals have violated every single promise they made during the 1980 election campaign". That is totally untrue.
Let me say to that hon. member that he has a golden opportunity, not only in this House, but within his party, to take the subject matters of energy and energy legislation before other members of his party in May of this year, discuss them at length and formulate resolutions of all sorts on all aspects of energy policy. I challenge the hon. member for Calgary Centre to go to that Conservative party policy convention in May and put forward resolutions, both on the leadership of his leader and on energy policies, and have them voted on. I challenge the hon. member to do that.
I challenge you to the same.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I would now like to make a few remarks about the petroleum compensation charge. Our pricing system is both realistic and fair. It takes into account the inescapable facts I mentioned earlier, particularly the need to provide an attractive incentive to encourage the development of new oil. Our blended pricing system differentiates between the varying developing costs of different types of oil.
Producers of what is commonly called old oil, oil discovered before December 31, 1980, faced comparatively lower costs than those of new oil producers. Therefore, they will get a price that will rise gradually and predictably at a fixed schedule to no more than 75 per cent of the international price.
Producers of new oil, oil discovered after December 31, 1981, synthetic oil and new frontier production, will get a higher price than that at the world level, but which will never rise above those levels. This price will provide a powerful incentive to producers to develop new oil supplies. These prices will in turn be blended into one made-in-Canada price that will apply in all regions of the country, regardless of what kind of oil is used, whether it is domestic or imported.
The petroleum compensation charge, which forms a major part of the bill before us, is extremely important. The program has played a vital role in protecting Atlantic Canada from the sudden shocks of international oil price increases that have characterized the past ten years. Members of the Conservative party may disagree with some aspects of that piece of legislation, but the bold fact remains, it has protected, and rightly protected, those people in Atlantic Canada.
As we know, all of Atlantic Canada's oil is imported. By compensating refiners for the difference between the international price they pay and the lower domestic price paid by refiners in other parts of Canada who have access to domestic production, the compensation program has provided untold economic benefits for Atlantic Canada.
Since the import compensation program was started by this government in 1974, it has paid out nationally a total of $13.7 billion in compensation. Atlantic Canada compensation to date has amounted to approximately $6.5 billion. This is a huge sum of money, but it is money wisely spent. If the compensation program did not exist, $6.5 billion would have been drained from the economy of Atlantic Canada. Instead, this money has stayed in the pockets of Atlantic Canadians to work for them.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The Conservative party in all parts of the country has shunned the petroleum compensation charge. It has closed its eyes to the concerns of Atlantic Canadians, and through its chief energy spokesmen has rejected development
April 26, 1982

of offshore resources in my region of the country. I object very strongly to that type of viewpoint, and that type of attitude.
The offshore resources will offer a significant contribution to Canada's energy security and to the economic development and prosperity of Canadians living in Nova Scotia and throughout the Atlantic area. For Nova Scotians, development of offshore energy resources offers a unique opportunity to build the lasting social and economic structures that can help to shape a prosperous future.
The agreement reached between the Government of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia established a strong, cooperative management regime capable of pursuing and harmonizing these energy and development objects in a manner consistent with the interests and responsibilities of each government and of industry, as well as of Nova Scotians and all Canadians.
In Nova Scotia many onshore opportunities will be provided as a result of offshore oil and gas resource activity. These opportunities will include new jobs and training in new skills, new business opportunities for industry and entrepreneurs, and significant new government revenues.
The Government of Canada's pricing and compensation system will play a major role in stimulating oil and natural gas development off the coast of my province. The compensation system will be the mechanism to ensure that producers of new oil in Atlantic Canada receive the new oil reference price for their production. This price will provide producers with returns that are competitive with returns offered anywhere else in the world. As such, the new oil reference price offers a powerful incentive to producers to explore aggressively for new supplies and develop significant new supplies of petroleum.
The petroleum compensation charge will remove an inequity that characterized the previous compensation system. Import compensation used to be funded from the government's general revenues, which were collected from the taxpayers. This meant that the amount of compensation effectively paid by Canadians bore no direct relationship to the amount of oil they consumed. The petroleum compensation charge eliminates this inequity, because it is a charge placed at the refinery level, which is then passed on to the consumers. Therefore, those who consume the most will contribute the most to offsetting the cost of compensation. However, the government will not, in spite of the innuendo of the Conservative Party of Canada, collect more from the petroleum compensation charge than is needed to cover the import subsidization and the new oil reference price supplements 1 have already mentioned. Mr. Speaker, this is only fair and it is only right.
It was very interesting to hear the Conservative party's energy critic speak in the House on the petroleum compensation charge. On the one hand he tried to have his party under its former leader, Mr. Stanfield, take credit for this program to assist Canadians using imported oil. On the other hand he
Energy Administration Act
blamed the government today for assisting Atlantic Canadians through the same program. So typical of the Conservative members, to speak out of both sides of their mouth, to give one position in one part of the country and yet give another position in another. You have to wonder who is fueling the separatist causes, Mr. Speaker.
How about the Minister of Energy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, may I deal for a few minutes with a major concern regarding shut-in oil.
You're speaking out of both sides of your mouth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Lately, there has been serious concern in western Canada that the oil import compensation program unintentionally encourages refiners to buy crude on the world spot market, resulting in large shut-ins of domestic light and heavy oil. The argument is that the combination of soft international prices and the compensation paid to refiners using imported oil has effectively subsidized the price of international oil below the price of domestic consumption, resulting in a surge of imports and reduced utilization of domestic crude oil.
Although there have been calls for a major restructuring of our import compensation program, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has stated he does not believe it is an important cause of the shut-in situation. Nor is he convinced that a change to the flat rate system of compensation would resolve the problem. Furthermore, current information does not indicate that there has been any surge in heavy or light crude imports. The compensation rates are reviewed regularly and adjusted to take into account fluctuations in the difference between the domestice price and the world price.
This situation has been discussed with the government of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and the minister has issued a statement on measures the government is prepared to take. They include reducing the oil export charge on heavy oil exports to the United States; providing longer term export licences to improve heavy oil marketability; ensuring that heavy oil exports are competitively priced; and asking the National Energy Board to make several important adjustments in its export regulations.
The minister has also made it clear to refiners in Quebec and Atlantic Canada that low-cost spot market oil should not be imported if this reduces the use of Canadian crude oil. He has asked them to limit imports of crude to minimum levels allowed under current contracts and, when renewing contracts, to take into account the likely availability of domestic crude, and to establish import volumes accordingly.
These are the steps, Mr. Speaker, the government is prepared to take at this time. However, our officials will continue

April 26, 1982
Energy Administration Act
to monitor the situation with provincial officials. If these measures do not produce the results we expect, the minister has indicated the Government of Canada is prepared to take further action.
Who are Canada's producers of oil and gas, Mr. Speaker? As of today, 65.5 per cent of all oil and gas production revenues accrue to foreigners, a figure not likely matched anywhere in the world, let alone in the developed world. Most of the largest oil and gas producers in Canada are foreign-owned and controlled. Before the introduction of the National Energy Program there was concern that with the development of expensive and technically difficult offshore and tar sands projects, the degree of foreign control would worsen. What national government, responsible for the well-being of all its citizens, could allow such a situation to continue?
The Canadian ownership special charge is the mechanism that will allow the government to participate more vigorously on behalf of all Canadians in the oil and gas industry. Certainly, this is not the sum total of our Canadianization program. In fact, the greater part of the program is designed to encourage the growth of Canadian private sector involvement in the industry.
The public sector role has been played with extraordinary success by Petro-Canada, the national oil company created by our government in 1976. I will not dwell at length about its achievements, because that is a subject matter for debate on another bill. Suffice to say, however, that since its inception in 1976 Petro-Canada has been the driving force behind 76 of the 128 wells that were drilled in the frontier regions. It was the first large Canadian landholder in the eastern offshore, the first Canadian-owned and controlled operator there, and has been a major participant in every major oil and gas field off the east coast. In its role as head of the Labrador project it is encouraging Canadian companies to get involved in east coast drilling. Despite the claims of some of the more extreme energy spokesmen, Petro-Canada's success rate for discovering oil and natural gas has been every bit as good as that of most companies, and better than many.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that it is very easy for members of the official opposition to criticize and tear down; to allow innuendo to circulate throughout the country; to say one thing in one part of Canada and to say another in a different region, but it is another thing to confront very serious issues, to provide an alternative, a commitment, and an answer to those wrongs, those inequities, and those inequalities. That is what we have attempted to do with the National Energy Program. This bill is part of this package and will implement a program which, I believe, is in the best interests of all the regions and all the people of Canada. I therefore urge all members of the House to support the bill.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief. It is not my intention to answer all the statements made by the hon. parliamentary secretary. It would take too long to straighten him out. I think he should find some technique other then the over worked strawman technique, where he says that the opposition stands for such and such a thing- although that is not so-and then tears apart the argument. That is a useful debating technique from time to time but, if it is used all the time, credibility suffers.
I should like to straighten the hon. member out on one particular point, and that is the import subsidy. It was the hon. Robert Stanfield who said in November, 1973, that we need a one-price system in this country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that it could not be done; this is reported in Hansard. A month later he found out that he could, and needed to do just that. I would remind the House that it was the Hon. Robert Stanfield who put forward the one-price system for which the hon. member is now taking credit.
The hon. member has told us not to worry, that the petroleum compensation charge will only be collected in amounts sufficient to pay for import compensation. I would ask him to examine the remarks made by the Hon. Donald Macdonald when he was minister of energy and imposed the export charge on crude oil. The funds were to be devoted to providing import compensation; to subsidize imports, so we would have a one-price system in Canada. Where are those funds today, Mr. Speaker? They go into general revenues.
In the budget of September, 1975, the Hon. John Turner imposed a seven cents per gallon excise tax on gasoline and told us that the money would go toward import compensation only. Where is that money going today? It goes into general revenues. It has disappeared. Now we have the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), and his parliamentary secretary, telling us not to worry, that the petroleum compensation charge is going toward import compensation. When two former ministers of the Liberal government made similar statements and their intentions have not been carried out, why should we take at face value the statement of the present minister?
My friend, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) tells us that if you are lied to once, the liar is at fault; if you get lied to twice then you are at fault. If you are lied to three times, then you are even more at fault. We just do not believe the minister, and we have good reason for that, Mr. Speaker.

PIPELINES-DELAY IN CONSTRUCTION OF TQM NATURAL GAS PIPELINE. (B) PRICE GUARANTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my question on April 20 to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was to ascertain when natural gas will be delivered by pipeline to the maritimes, and what the government is going to do to ensure that it will be a competitive energy form.
The minister indicated that the price to the consumer in the maritimes will be maintained at the same level as the price in Toronto. I would like the minister to give the House an indication of what the Toronto city gate price, generally speaking, will be in relation to other energy forms. Can it fluctuate widely after the expiration of the Ottawa-Alberta energy agreement in 1986 or 1987, and are any safeguards built in with respect to the price change which might take place at that time? Is the minister satisfied that the price of natural gas will compete with oil or electricity in the maritimes, and, for industrial users, will natural gas be able to compete with heavy
16638

April 26, 1982
Adjournment Debate
fuel oils? I would appreciate it if the minister would elaborate on what the government is prepared to do to make natural gas competitive with electricity and oil? If the cost of the pipeline exceeds expectations will it be subsidized?
Finally, is it the policy of the government to use local workers, suppliers and trades people whenever possible, and thereby use this pipeline as a development tool in the Atlantic provinces?
In conclusion, will the minister confirm whether or not there is provision for mandatory review of the pipeline project by the National Energy Board once it is completed to Quebec City, and what if anything is the significance of this provision? I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the parliamentary secretary, for coming here tonight to respond to my question.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PIPELINES-DELAY IN CONSTRUCTION OF TQM NATURAL GAS PIPELINE. (B) PRICE GUARANTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on many occasions the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has stated that the extension of the natural gas distribution system to the maritimes is one of the top priorities of the federal government as it is committed to the reduction of oil dependence in the Atlantic region and it believes that a gas pipeline affords one of the best approaches to this objective.
With specific regard to the price of natural gas to maritime consumers, I might direct hon. members to the National Energy Program report. There it is clearly stated:
The gas prices in the National Energy Program should provide a basis for commercial viability of the line and associated distribution systems. The pricing system should establish prices at the city gate in Halifax at the same level as those in southern Ontario and Quebec.
On January 13, 1982 the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources issued a policy statement on natural gas pricing subsequent to the September 1, 1981 Canada-Alberta agreement on energy pricing and taxation and the National Energy Board's recommendations on developmental prices.
This January policy announcement stated in part that for the purpose of pricing, the existing TransCanada pipelines eastern zone will be extended to include the areas of Quebec and the maritimes which will be served by the trans-Quebec and Maritimes pipeline. City gate prices in markets east of Toronto will be the same as the Toronto city gate price for the same type of gas service. It stated also that to encourage rapid expansion and build-up of new natural gas markets in Quebec and the maritimes, beginning November 1, 1982 developmental prices will be prescribed.
With regard to this second point, the energy minister has stated that this pricing regime, which will be implemented on November 1, 1982, will provide distributors with a limited holiday from payment of certain transmission costs, thereby encouraging eligible distributors to expand gas markets in Quebec and the maritimes quickly and aggressively.
Last month the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced the implementation of the distribution system expansion program, another major off-oil initiative under the National Energy Program.
In summary it can be noted that the government has implemented a number of measures to ensure the viability of natural gas marketing into the maritimes. The Toronto price zone is to be extended through to the east coast so that consumers in the maritimes will have access to gas at prices comparable with consumers in Ontario who, in turn, will get their natural gas supplies at a price equivalent to 65 per cent of the oil price. The developmental price will provide an additional incentive for new customers. The distribution system expansion program will assist distributors in financing facilities into new marketing areas. And the Canada oil substitution program will provide the home owner with a significant part of the cost of converting his oil heating unit to natural gas.
All of these measures are directed toward energy supply security for maritimers at prices on a par with those throughout the rest of Canada.

COMMITTEES OF THE HOUSE-(A) APPEARANCE OF MINISTER OF FINANCE BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE. (B) REQUEST FOR VERIFICATION OF RUMOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my concern tonight arises from a question I asked last Wednesday of the chairman of the House committee on finance, and economic affairs. I asked a question with respect to the attendance of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) at finance committee hearings. At that time I wanted a commitment from the chairman that the minister would appear on April 29 and April 30 and once more in the first week of May.
It appears that, as a result of a steering committee hearing tonight, the minister will appear on April 29 and April 30 but he will not make any commitment with respect to May at all. He wants to continue his practice of being "absent Allan".
We have a committee system in this House whereby ministers are required to appear before committees to justify their estimates. The minister in this Parliament, that is this Parliament commencing as a result of the February, 1980 election, has appeared before the committee to justify his estimates once. That was December 4, 1980 when he appeared on supplementary estimates B for an hour and a half.
The minister has done everything in his power to avoid his estimates or his department being scrutinized, and to ensure that he never has to answer, or say what his policy is, or justify a thing to the committee. If other ministers acted in the same manner as this minister, the committee system would totally break down. I understand the position of the minister, that the committee system is not worth much the way it is organized. We certainly need a change in the system, but no system can work if the minister refuses, with one excuse after another, to appear.
April 26, 1982

The minister was supposed to appear before committee on April 20. He promised to be there on that date. But, just before the meeting, he found a reason to go to Toronto, it was alleged, to inquire of businessmen concerning his iniquitous budget of November 12. There were no meetings with businessmen on April 20. The minister ducked the committee, as he has been ducking the people of Canada. He is a duck of a minister. He is a minister who refuses to account, refuses to explain, refuses to come clean. He files green papers with respect to disclosure and how the budget should be forthcoming. He files other documents in the House but refuses to come to committee and refuses to explain his position.
He is a minister who would like to remain silent. He likes to have his selected few around him so that he can make a press release and say things, such as he said in the House on December 18, that he would take certain questions on the budget to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. But he never bothered making a reference because he knew there were hon. members on this side of the House who would ask some pretty penetrating questions. The Minister of Finance does not want to explain, does not want to come clean; he wants to hide.
We expect him to appear before the committee on April 29 and April 30. We expect him to come forth the first week in May. Unless we see that, we will have to take action in the House other than the action I have taken tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: COMMITTEES OF THE HOUSE-(A) APPEARANCE OF MINISTER OF FINANCE BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE. (B) REQUEST FOR VERIFICATION OF RUMOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) are totally incorrect. Far from ducking his responsibilities, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) offered an alternative date to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs as soon as it became apparent that he would have to postpone his appearance before the committee on the main estimates because of his commitments in another city. Indeed, the minister responded favourably to the committee's suggestion that he appear twice. Prior to the hon. member's question in the House, he conveyed to the committee his agreement to appear on April 29 and April 30, 1982. Contrary to the implication in the statement of the hon. member for Mississauga South, the minister has not refused to appear before the committee with respect to his policy, but has appeared when asked. He recently testified before the committee on Bill C-97 to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act.
As has already been indicated, the minister went to Toronto on the evening of April 20 because he and other ministers were to meet early the next day with representatives of the business community. In fact, there were two meetings, morning and afternoon discussions, with a total of some 40 private sector representatives. The Toronto meetings were the eighth, and ninth in an ongoing set of consultations on the economy with representatives of the private sector.
The Minister of Finance and other participating ministers have found that these meetings provided an excellent opportunity for an exchange of views with the private sector on the
Adjournment Debate
current economic situation. The meetings have covered the difficulties encountered due to the current recession and inflation, with consequential high interest rates. The discussions dealt with how to tackle these problems, with support being given to the broad direction of the current stance on monetary and fiscal policy. If is the government's intention, of course, to continue with consultations on economic matters in the weeks and months ahead.
This commitment to consultation on economic development matters was set out in the budget paper entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s", as well as being reiterated at meetings currently being held. Additional evidence of the government's intentions in this regard has been provided through the just recently published green paper on the budget process.
I repeat that the remarks made by the hon. member for Mississauga South are totally incorrect and, at best, despicable.

AGRICULTURE-BEEF STABILIZATION PROGRAM. (B) REQUEST PAYMENTS NOT BE LINKED WITH SUPPLY MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the beef producers of Canada have been going through a very strenuous economic time in the last several months. It was my hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) would perhaps have stayed tonight to give some answers to some very pertinent questions. Instead, he has left the parliamentary secretary, who is an hon. gentleman, to answer the questions. I presume I will probably get nothing more than a canned speech.
The beef producers in western Canada are very disturbed. The minister promised eight or nine weeks ago that he would be making an announcement within two or three weeks. He made the same statement four or five weeks ago in Calgary.
On April 2, I attempted to get an announcement from the minister as to what government policy was with regard to stabilization payments and what his plans were. The minister stated that he believed he would make a statement in three weeks. That was on April 2, which is three weeks and three days ago. Although the minister has had three weeks, plus three days of grace, we still do not seem to be receiving any answers. Calls are still coming in every day.
The minister has confirmed that the stabilization pay-out has no connection whatsoever to the apparent proposals the minister has in mind for the beef industry. Therefore, there is no reason whatsoever for the minister to withhold any announcement on the pay-out. Furthermore, after he makes the announcement, I presume he will have to go to Cabinet to get approval.
The minister has the industry in a real quandary. Prior to the end of last year, he sent out a questionnaire. It turned out to be a fiasco. The questionnaire was delivered to only 87,000

April 26, 1982
Adjournment Debate
beef producers; we recognize that the dairy industry contributes approximately 15 per cent to the beef industry. Nevertheless, he sent the questionnaire to only 15,000 dairymen. According to the 1976 census, there are 165,000 beef producers in Canada. This means that a great number of beef producers were overlooked entirely by this questionnaire. This certainly left a question in the minds of beef producers in my province where there are 47,000. Some of them did not receive a questionnaire, while others received two or three. This was nothing short of a farce. Of course, some of the feedlots where large numbers of beef are produced were overlooked entirely. Why has the minister not released the figures on his questionnaire, incorrect as they may be?
1 also understand that he conducted a private poll of his own; there has been no answer to that. Why has he not given us those figures? Why has he not released the Anderson-Vandermeulen report? Why has he not agreed to work with the cattlemen and the industry on future programs? He should take them into his confidence and negotiate a plan with them.
Why does the minister have such a mistrust of Canadian cattlemen? Why does he not accept any of the new proposals that beef producers make? The main question which must be asked is, why; why does he not give cattlemen some answers? They are becoming very disturbed and time is running out.

Mir. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture): Mr. Speaker, I hope that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) will nonetheless accept a reply from the Parliamentary Secretary, considering that the minister has had to leave the House to attend to other business.
The 1981 beef sales stabilization year ended on December 31, 1981. Provisional estimates indicate that no payment is required at the 90 per cent statutory level provided for under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. The market price for beef sold in 1981, valued at $75.03 per hundredweight, is lower than the price established in 1980, that is, $74.37 per hundredweight. In figuring out the support price, the following elements must be included in the cash costs of production: feed
grains, feeder calves, interest on operating capital, and other costs related to veterinary services, public services, insurance, hired labour, litter, and repairs to buildings and equipment.
In 1981, the cost of feed increased 20 per cent because of high prices for grain, interest rates increased 14 per cent and miscellaneous costs, 9 per cent. However, the price of feeder calves, the most important factor for feed lot operators, dropped 7 per cent in 1981, compared with 1980. The drop in price was sufficient to compensate for increases in the cash cost of other aspects of production. As a result, preliminary figures indicate that cash costs for raising slaughter cattle in 1981 are similar to those in 1980.
As the minister indicated in the House on April 2, he met with representatives of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association on February 26, 1982, to discuss possibilities for assistance under the Act. Although final figures were not available at that time, the representatives realized that assistance at the 90 per cent level was not justified, and that is why they subsequently requested assistance at the 95 per cent level.
Market prices have remained more or less unchanged during the last three years: $76.44 per cwt in 1979, $76.37 in 1980 and $75.03 in 1981, thus causing producers to exhaust their reserves in order to survive during this difficult period. The minister and his colleagues are examining the feasibility of offering support payments for cattle sold in 1981, and an announcement will be made shortly in this respect. Mr. Speaker, I may conclude by saying that the minister has always worked in close co-operation with Canadian beef producer associations across the country, and I believe he will continue to do so in the best interests of cattlemen in this country.
